You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high — the average cost is set by the rule, not by your judgment. The key feature is it removes the timing decision.
conceptChoices: Investing a fixed dollar amount on a fixed schedule regardless of market conditions
Investing more when the market drops and less when it rises
Calculating the average cost basis of all your investments
Spreading your money across multiple asset classes
correctConceptChoice: Investing a fixed dollar amount on a fixed schedule regardless of market conditions

promptTemplate: According to Vanguard's well-known 2012 study, lump-sum investing beats DCA on returns about...
explanationTemplate: Per Vanguard's 2012 study 'Dollar-Cost Averaging Just Means Taking Risk Later,' lump-sum investing outperformed DCA in approximately two-thirds of historical 10-year windows. The reason: markets trend up more often than down, so getting fully invested earlier captures more upside on average.
conceptChoices: Roughly 1/3 of the time
Roughly 2/3 of the time
Roughly 9/10 of the time
Lump-sum never beats DCA
correctConceptChoice: Roughly 2/3 of the time

promptTemplate: If lump-sum statistically wins on returns, why is DCA the right choice for most retail investors?
explanationTemplate: DCA wins on behavior. Lump-sum requires investing all at once — and most retail investors who try this hesitate, wait for a 'better entry,' get scared by a dip, and ultimately invest less than they planned. DCA removes the decision (and the emotion) by automating it. The strategy that gets executed beats the strategy that's theoretically optimal but never followed.
conceptChoices: DCA always has higher returns when accounting for fees
Most retail investors who try lump-sum hesitate, time the market poorly, and end up under-invested — DCA removes that decision
DCA is tax-advantaged in ways lump-sum isn't
The Vanguard study was disproven by later research
correctConceptChoice: Most retail investors who try lump-sum hesitate, time the market poorly, and end up under-invested — DCA removes that decision

promptTemplate: When is DCA most clearly the right choice (even setting aside the behavioral angle)?
explanationTemplate: Recurring paycheck contributions are textbook DCA — money arrives in chunks, you can't lump-sum what you don't yet have. 401(k) contributions, automated brokerage transfers on payday, and IRA monthly contributions all naturally fit the DCA model. For genuine one-time windfalls (inheritance, bonus, home sale proceeds), the lump-sum argument applies more directly — but only if you can actually pull the trigger.
conceptChoices: When you have a one-time windfall like an inheritance
When you receive income on a recurring schedule (paycheck, monthly contributions) — DCA is automatic, not a choice
Only when the market is dropping
Only in tax-advantaged accounts
correctConceptChoice: When you receive income on a recurring schedule (paycheck, monthly contributions) — DCA is automatic, not a choice

promptTemplate: You have a $12,000 windfall and plan to invest it. You think about lump-summing it but want to 'wait for the dip.' Six months later you've invested $3,000 and the market is up 8%. What's the cost of waiting?
explanationTemplate: The $9,000 still sitting in cash missed an 8% gain (~$720) — and worse, you've fallen into the 'wait for the dip' trap that delays indefinitely. An automated 12-month DCA plan would have already invested ~$6,000 and captured part of the rally. The behavioral lesson: when you can't execute lump-sum, DCA's discipline beats trying to time the market every time.
conceptChoices: Zero — you're being prudent by waiting
About $720 in missed gains on the $9,000 still in cash — plus the hidden cost of continuing to wait for a dip that may not come
Only the inflation cost on the cash
Impossible to estimate without knowing the future
correctConceptChoice: About $720 in missed gains on the $9,000 still in cash — plus the hidden cost of continuing to wait for a dip that may not come

promptTemplate: Your portfolio is worth ${{portfolioValue}}. Your fund has a {{expenseRatio}}% expense ratio. How much do you pay in fees per year?
explanationTemplate: Portfolio × expense ratio. ${{portfolioValue}} × {{expenseRatio}}% = ${{answer}}/year.

promptTemplate: Compare Fund A ({{expenseRatioA}}%) vs Fund B ({{expenseRatioB}}%) on a ${{portfolioValue}} portfolio. What's the annual fee difference?
explanationTemplate: (ratioA − ratioB) × portfolio. ({{expenseRatioA}}% − {{expenseRatioB}}%) × ${{portfolioValue}} = ${{answer}}/year saved.

promptTemplate: An index fund charges {{expenseRatio}}% on a ${{portfolioValue}} portfolio. Annual fee?
explanationTemplate: ${{portfolioValue}} × {{expenseRatio}}% = ${{answer}}. Index funds typically charge under 0.2%.

promptTemplate: Over 10 years, a {{expenseRatioA}}% fund vs a {{expenseRatioB}}% fund on a ${{portfolioValue}} portfolio. How much MORE do you pay in fees (ignoring growth)?
explanationTemplate: (rateA − rateB) × portfolio × 10 years = ${{answer}}. And this ignores the lost compounding.

promptTemplate: Rule of thumb: every 0.5% in extra fees costs ~10% of your 30-year final balance. If your projected balance is ${{projectedBalance}} and you're paying {{extraFee}}% more in fees than necessary, roughly how much are you losing?
explanationTemplate: Lost balance ≈ projected × extra fee × 20. ${{projectedBalance}} × {{extraFee}}% × 20 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Monthly essentials: rent ${{rent}}, food ${{food}}, insurance ${{insurance}}, transport ${{transport}}. What's your essential monthly expense total?
explanationTemplate: Add them: ${{rent}} + ${{food}} + ${{insurance}} + ${{transport}} = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Your essential expenses are ${{essentials}}/month. What's your 6-month emergency fund target?
explanationTemplate: Essentials × 6. ${{essentials}} × 6 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You have ${{savings}} saved. Essentials cost ${{essentials}}/month. How many months of runway does that give you?
explanationTemplate: Savings ÷ essentials. ${{savings}} ÷ ${{essentials}} = ~{{answer}} months.

promptTemplate: You have ${{savings}} saved with ${{essentials}}/month in essentials. If you cut ${{cutAmount}} from non-essentials, how many months of runway do you gain?
explanationTemplate: New runway = savings ÷ (essentials − cut). Gain = new − original = {{answer}} extra months.

promptTemplate: You want a ${{target}} emergency fund. You have ${{currentSaved}} saved and can add ${{monthlyContribution}}/month. How many months until you hit the target?
explanationTemplate: (target − current) ÷ monthly. (${{target}} − ${{currentSaved}}) ÷ ${{monthlyContribution}} = ~{{answer}} months.

promptTemplate: What is the '1% rule' for rental properties?
explanationTemplate: The 1% rule is a quick screening test: monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price for a property to have any chance of cash-flowing after all real expenses. A $300k property needs $3,000/month rent to pass. Most properties in HCOL US metros fail this test in 2026 — they're appreciation plays, not cash flow.
conceptChoices: Monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price as a quick cash-flow screen
1% of the property value should be set aside annually for repairs
1% is the maximum landlord profit margin allowed by federal law
The mortgage should be at most 1% of the rent
correctConceptChoice: Monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price as a quick cash-flow screen

promptTemplate: Which of these is NOT a normal monthly expense for a rental property's cash-flow analysis?
explanationTemplate: Property taxes, insurance, mortgage P&I, vacancy reserve, and maintenance reserve are all legitimate monthly expenses. The 'sale price' is a future event, not a current expense — and crucially, a positive sale price is not income you can spend monthly. Real-estate beginners often forget reserves and overstate cash flow.
conceptChoices: Property taxes
Mortgage interest
The eventual sale price of the property
Vacancy reserve
correctConceptChoice: The eventual sale price of the property

promptTemplate: Roughly what % of monthly rent should be set aside for vacancy + maintenance + capex (capital expenditures) in a realistic cash-flow model?
explanationTemplate: Conventional landlord rules of thumb: ~8% vacancy reserve (1 month vacant per year), ~10% maintenance, ~5-10% capex. Combined: ~25% of gross rent disappears into reserves before you even count mortgage and taxes. First-time landlords routinely miss this and overstate monthly cash flow.
conceptChoices: 1-3% — rentals are mostly hands-off
5-10% — only major repairs need reserves
~25% combined (vacancy ~8% + maintenance ~10% + capex ~5-10%)
Reserves aren't necessary if you self-manage
correctConceptChoice: ~25% combined (vacancy ~8% + maintenance ~10% + capex ~5-10%)

promptTemplate: A property collects $2,500/month rent. After mortgage ($1,500), taxes + insurance ($350), and 25% in combined reserves ($625), what's the monthly cash flow?
explanationTemplate: $2,500 − $1,500 − $350 − $625 = $25/month. Barely positive — and one major capex event (HVAC, roof, water heater) erases years of that cash flow. Most 'investment properties' people excitedly buy on gross yield numbers look like this once real reserves are applied.
conceptChoices: +$650/month (everything after mortgage)
+$25/month — barely positive, vulnerable to any single capex event
−$200/month
Positive long-term because property appreciates
correctConceptChoice: +$25/month — barely positive, vulnerable to any single capex event

promptTemplate: A property has negative monthly cash flow after all real expenses, but the realtor pitches it as a good investment because 'real estate always appreciates in this neighborhood.' What's the most accurate way to describe this?
explanationTemplate: A property that doesn't cash-flow is a speculative bet on future price appreciation — not an investment in the rental-income sense. Speculation isn't wrong, but it's a different risk profile: you're committing capital and paying out-of-pocket every month, hoping for a future capital gain. Be honest with yourself about which game you're actually playing.
conceptChoices: It's an investment as long as the realtor knows the neighborhood
It's a speculation on future appreciation, not a rental investment — different risk profile, and you should be honest about which game you're playing
It's automatically a good buy because real estate always appreciates
It's a tax shelter regardless of cash flow
correctConceptChoice: It's a speculation on future appreciation, not a rental investment — different risk profile, and you should be honest about which game you're playing

promptTemplate: You've saved ${{currentSavings}} for retirement. Your current salary is ${{currentSalary}}. What's your savings multiple?
explanationTemplate: Savings ÷ salary. ${{currentSavings}} ÷ ${{currentSalary}} = {{answer}}% (i.e. ~{{answer}}/100 × salary).

promptTemplate: Fidelity's rule: by age {{targetAge}}, you should have {{targetMultiple}}× your salary saved. If your salary is ${{currentSalary}}, what's your target savings?
explanationTemplate: Salary × multiple. ${{currentSalary}} × {{targetMultiple}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You're {{currentAge}} years old, earning ${{currentSalary}}, with ${{currentSavings}} saved. Your age-based target is {{targetMultiple}}× salary. How much is your savings gap?
explanationTemplate: Target = salary × multiple. Gap = target − current = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You're ${{gap}} behind your savings target. You want to close the gap in {{years}} years. How much extra per month do you need to save?
explanationTemplate: Gap ÷ (years × 12). ${{gap}} ÷ ({{years}} × 12) = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Salary ${{currentSalary}}, current contribution rate {{currentRate}}%. You want to bump to {{targetRate}}%. How much MORE per month do you contribute?
explanationTemplate: (target − current) × salary ÷ 12. ({{targetRate}}% − {{currentRate}}%) × ${{currentSalary}} ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You take out a ${{loanAmount}} loan. Monthly payment ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}} months. What's your 'interest tax' (total interest ÷ loan amount, as %)?
explanationTemplate: Total = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest tax = interest ÷ loan × 100 = {{answer}}%.

promptTemplate: Buy now: ${{monthlyPayment}}/mo × {{numMonths}} months = total. Or save ${{savedAmount}}/month for {{saveMonths}} months and pay cash for ${{purchasePrice}}. How much do you save by waiting?
explanationTemplate: Borrow total = ${{monthlyPayment}} × {{numMonths}}. Cash = ${{purchasePrice}}. Saving = borrow − cash = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Monthly income ${{monthlyIncome}}. Current monthly debt payments ${{currentDebt}}. You're considering a ${{newPayment}}/month car loan. What's your new DTI ratio?
explanationTemplate: (currentDebt + newPayment) ÷ income × 100 = (${{currentDebt}} + ${{newPayment}}) ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = {{answer}}%.

promptTemplate: Credit card balance ${{balance}} at {{apr}}% APR. You pay ${{totalPayment}} this month ({{minPayment}} minimum + ${{extraPayment}} extra). How much of your payment goes to principal (after interest)?
explanationTemplate: Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 1200. Principal portion = total payment − interest = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} balance at {{apr}}% APR. You pay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month. After interest, how much of that payment actually reduces principal?
explanationTemplate: Principal slice = monthly payment − (balance × APR ÷ 1200). The smaller this number, the longer your payoff. If it's small, your payment is mostly servicing interest, not shrinking what you owe.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} balance at {{apr}}% APR. You pay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month. About how many months until it's paid off?
explanationTemplate: Months ≈ ln(payment / (payment − balance × APR ÷ 1200)) / ln(1 + APR ÷ 1200). The exact formula is logarithmic — the higher the interest fraction of your payment, the longer the timeline.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} balance at {{apr}}% APR. Bumping your payment from $150 to ${{monthlyPayment}}/month, what's your new payoff time in months?
explanationTemplate: Even a modest payment bump dramatically shrinks payoff time because (1) more principal goes to the balance, and (2) lower balance means less interest each subsequent month — the effect compounds.

promptTemplate: Your $5,000 balance at 22% APR will take ~52 months to pay off at $150/month. Bump to $200/month — roughly how long?
explanationTemplate: $200/month payoff: ~34 months. The extra $50/month cuts about 18 months (1.5 years) off the payoff — because each $50 of extra principal also reduces every future month's interest charge.
conceptChoices: About 45 months (modest improvement)
About 34 months — roughly 18 months shorter than at $150/mo
About 51 months still — the extra is too small to matter
Less than 12 months — extra payment is hugely powerful
correctConceptChoice: About 34 months — roughly 18 months shorter than at $150/mo

promptTemplate: Realistic scenario: ${{balance}} credit card balance at {{apr}}% APR. You pay ${{monthlyPayment}}/month. After interest, how much principal do you actually pay down this month?
explanationTemplate: Principal reduction this month = payment − (balance × APR ÷ 1200). At high balances + high APRs, even a $150-180 payment may only reduce principal by $20-50 — which is why minimum-payment-only borrowers stay in debt for years (often decades).

promptTemplate: You transfer a ${{balance}} balance to a new card charging {{feePct}}% transfer fee. How much is the fee?
explanationTemplate: Fee = balance × fee%. ${{balance}} × {{feePct}}% = ${{answer}}. Typical balance-transfer fees are 3-5% (per major card issuers); the lower end is more common on premium cards.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} balance at {{oldApr}}% APR. If you avoid interest for the next {{promoMonths}} months (via a 0% balance-transfer promo), how much interest do you save?
explanationTemplate: Interest avoided = balance × old APR × promo months ÷ 12. ${{balance}} × {{oldApr}}% × {{promoMonths}}/12 = ${{answer}}. This is the upside of the transfer — to be compared against the transfer fee.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} balance at {{oldApr}}% APR. Transfer to a 0% card with a {{feePct}}% fee and a {{promoMonths}}-month promo. Net benefit (interest saved minus fee)?
explanationTemplate: Net = interest avoided − fee = (balance × oldApr × promoMonths ÷ 1200) − (balance × feePct ÷ 100) = ${{answer}}. Positive means the transfer saves money; the bigger the spread between APR and fee, the better.

promptTemplate: A balance transfer offers an 18-month 0% promo with a 3% fee. Your old card APR is 18%. What's the minimum APR at which the transfer becomes worth it?
explanationTemplate: Breakeven: fee% = old APR × promo months ÷ 12 → 3% = APR × 18/12 → APR = 2%. ANY APR above 2% beats the 3% fee over an 18-month window. In practice, if you're paying credit-card-level APR (18%+), an 18-month 3%-fee transfer is a strong win. Shorter promos and higher fees tighten the math.
conceptChoices: Anything above 2% APR — at 18 months of 0%, the math beats a 3% fee very easily
At least 10% APR — fees usually win at lower rates
At least 22% APR — only worth it on credit-card rates
Always worth it regardless of APR
correctConceptChoice: Anything above 2% APR — at 18 months of 0%, the math beats a 3% fee very easily

promptTemplate: You transfer ${{balance}} to a 0% card with a {{promoMonths}}-month promo and a {{feePct}}% fee. To pay it off entirely before the promo ends, what monthly payment do you need?
explanationTemplate: Monthly payment = (balance × (1 + fee%)) ÷ promo months. You're paying down the transferred balance + the upfront fee over the 0% window. If you can't sustain this payment, the leftover balance hits the new card's regular APR after the promo ends — eroding the savings.

promptTemplate: Debt A: {{aprA}}% APR. Debt B: {{aprB}}% APR. Under the avalanche method, by how many percentage points does the priority debt's rate exceed the other?
explanationTemplate: Higher APR − lower APR = {{answer}} percentage points. That's why avalanche targets the higher rate.

promptTemplate: You have ${{extraPayment}} extra/month to pay debt. Putting it on a {{highRate}}% card vs a {{lowRate}}% card. How much MORE monthly interest do you save by targeting the higher rate?
explanationTemplate: Extra × (highRate − lowRate) ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = ${{answer}}/month extra savings via avalanche.

promptTemplate: You have a ${{extraPayment}}/month surplus and two debts: ${{balanceA}} at {{aprA}}% APR and ${{balanceB}} at {{aprB}}% APR. Snowball targets the smaller balance. By how much more annual interest does avalanche save than snowball?
explanationTemplate: Avalanche puts ${{extraPayment}} on A (higher rate). Snowball puts it on B. Annual diff = extra × (aprA − aprB) ÷ 100 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: On a ${{balance}} balance, the monthly interest at {{apr}}% APR is what?
explanationTemplate: Balance × APR ÷ 1200. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Over 24 months, avalanche saves ${{monthlySaving}}/month more than snowball. What's the 'psychology premium' you pay (total) for the snowball approach?
explanationTemplate: Monthly difference × 24. ${{monthlySaving}} × 24 = ${{answer}} 'paid' for psychological wins.

promptTemplate: What is the 'APR' on a loan or credit card?
explanationTemplate: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the annualized interest rate plus most fees, expressed as a single number for comparison across lenders. By federal Reg Z (Truth in Lending Act, per CFPB), every lender must disclose APR, making it the standard comparison metric on loans and credit cards.
conceptChoices: The annualized interest rate plus required fees, used as a standard comparison number across lenders (per Reg Z)
The monthly interest rate, multiplied by 100
Only the fees on a loan, not the interest
The interest rate after compounding is applied
correctConceptChoice: The annualized interest rate plus required fees, used as a standard comparison number across lenders (per Reg Z)

promptTemplate: A loan with {{apr}}% APR has what monthly interest rate?
explanationTemplate: Per-period rate = APR ÷ periods/year. For monthly billing (cards, mortgages): APR ÷ 12. {{apr}}% ÷ 12 = {{answer}}% monthly.

promptTemplate: Your card balance is ${{balance}} at {{apr}}% APR carried all year (simple-interest estimate, no compounding). What's the annual interest cost?
explanationTemplate: Annual cost (simple) = balance × APR. ${{balance}} × {{apr}}% = ${{answer}}. Real billing with monthly compounding is slightly higher (the APR-vs-APY gap), but APR is still the right comparison number across cards.

promptTemplate: Loan A: 8.5% rate + 2% origination fee. Loan B: 9.5% rate, no fees. The advertised APR captures...
explanationTemplate: APR (per Reg Z / Truth in Lending) includes required fees expressed as an annual rate. Loan A's APR ≈ 9.7% (rate + amortized fee); Loan B's APR = 9.5%. Loan B is the better deal — but only because the standardized APR captures the apples-to-apples comparison. Comparing just the 'rate' would mislead you.
conceptChoices: Only the interest rate — origination fees are separate
Both the interest rate and required fees, expressed as an annual rate — which is why APR is the standard comparison number
Only the fees, not the rate
Whichever number the lender wants to advertise
correctConceptChoice: Both the interest rate and required fees, expressed as an annual rate — which is why APR is the standard comparison number

promptTemplate: A loan with ${{monthlyPayment}} monthly payment over {{numMonths}} months. How much total interest do you pay over the life of the loan?
explanationTemplate: Total paid = payment × months. Interest = total − loan amount. The APR you signed for produces this total — high APR + long term = bigger 'interest tax' on what you borrowed.

promptTemplate: What is APY on a savings account or CD?
explanationTemplate: APY (Annual Percentage Yield) is the rate WITH compounding included — the actual annual return on your savings. By federal law (Truth in Savings Act / Reg DD, per FDIC), banks must disclose APY on savings products, making it the right comparison number for savings accounts, money market funds, and CDs.
conceptChoices: The rate WITH compounding included — the actual annual return on your savings (per Reg DD)
The interest rate before tax
The rate banks pay to other banks
The minimum balance fee
correctConceptChoice: The rate WITH compounding included — the actual annual return on your savings (per Reg DD)

promptTemplate: You have ${{balance}} in a high-yield savings account at {{apy}}% APY. How much interest do you earn in one year?
explanationTemplate: Annual interest = balance × APY. ${{balance}} × {{apy}}% = ${{answer}}/year. In 2026, top HYSAs pay around 4-4.5% APY (per HYSA tracking sites like Bankrate and DepositAccounts) — orders of magnitude better than the 0.01% you'd get at a major brick-and-mortar bank.

promptTemplate: Your big-bank savings account pays 0.01% APY. A high-yield savings account pays {{apy}}% APY. On a ${{balance}} balance, how much more interest does the HYSA earn per year?
explanationTemplate: HYSA: ${{balance}} × {{apy}}% ≈ ${{answer}}. Big-bank savings: ${{balance}} × 0.01% = pennies. The gap is essentially the full HYSA payout — free money for the act of moving the account.

promptTemplate: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how many years does it take for cash in a {{apy}}% APY savings account to double?
explanationTemplate: 72 ÷ APY ≈ years to double. At {{apy}}% APY: 72 ÷ {{apy}} ≈ {{answer}} years. (Rule of 72 works the same for savings APY as for investment returns — it's just the math of compounding.)

promptTemplate: Bank A advertises 4.50% APR with monthly compounding. Bank B advertises 4.55% APY. Which actually pays more?
explanationTemplate: Bank A's 4.50% APR with monthly compounding produces APY ≈ 4.59%. So Bank A actually pays slightly more — but the difference is tiny (~$5/year on $10k). The compounding-frequency effect is small at these rates; what matters far more is choosing between 0.01% and 4-5% accounts, not which 4-5% account.
conceptChoices: Bank B — its 4.55% number is higher
Bank A — 4.50% APR with monthly compounding ≈ 4.59% APY, slightly higher than B's 4.55%
They pay exactly the same
Bank A — APR always beats APY
correctConceptChoice: Bank A — 4.50% APR with monthly compounding ≈ 4.59% APY, slightly higher than B's 4.55%

promptTemplate: A {{numPayments}}-payment BNPL plan of ${{paymentAmount}} each. Total cost?
explanationTemplate: {{numPayments}} × ${{paymentAmount}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You're on a 4-payment BNPL plan of ${{paymentAmount}} per payment. You miss one — the late fee is $35. What's your TOTAL out-of-pocket cost?
explanationTemplate: 4 × ${{paymentAmount}} payment + $35 late fee = ${{answer}}. Late fees turn 'free' BNPL into expensive credit.

promptTemplate: You bought a ${{originalPrice}} item on BNPL and missed one payment, triggering a $35 late fee. What percentage of the original price was the surcharge?
explanationTemplate: Late fee ÷ original price × 100 = surcharge. $35 ÷ ${{originalPrice}} × 100 = {{answer}}%. A 'free' BNPL plan with one missed payment can add a hefty surcharge — especially on small purchases.

promptTemplate: Three active BNPL plans: ${{paymentA}}/mo, ${{paymentB}}/mo, ${{paymentC}}/mo. What's your total invisible monthly BNPL debt obligation?
explanationTemplate: Sum it up: ${{paymentA}} + ${{paymentB}} + ${{paymentC}} = ${{answer}}/month. Not on your credit card statement — that's the trap.

promptTemplate: You use BNPL plans averaging ${{monthlyBnpl}}/month all year. What's your annual BNPL spending?
explanationTemplate: Monthly × 12. ${{monthlyBnpl}} × 12 = ${{answer}}/year of invisible BNPL spending.

promptTemplate: You found an apartment for ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Using the 28% rule, what minimum monthly gross income do you need to afford it?
explanationTemplate: Min income = rent ÷ 0.28. ${{monthlyRent}} ÷ 0.28 = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Your monthly GROSS income is ${{monthlyGross}}. Using the 28% rule, what's the maximum PITI (principal + interest + tax + insurance) you can afford?
explanationTemplate: Max PITI = gross monthly × 28% (per Fannie Mae 28/36 rule). ${{monthlyGross}} × 28% = ${{answer}}/month — your ceiling for total housing cost including taxes and insurance.

promptTemplate: Your monthly P&I budget is ${{pAndI}}. At a 6% mortgage rate (factor 0.006 per $1 of loan), how much loan can you support?
explanationTemplate: Loan amount = P&I ÷ rate factor. ${{pAndI}} ÷ 0.006 = ${{answer}}. The rate factor changes with rate: 0.0054 at 5%, 0.006 at 6%, 0.0067 at 7% — each percentage point higher costs you ~10-15% in supported loan amount.

promptTemplate: You're putting less than 20% down, so PMI kicks in. Loan amount ${{loanAmount}}, PMI rate {{pmiPct}}% annual. What's the monthly PMI cost?
explanationTemplate: Monthly PMI = loan × PMI% ÷ 1200. ${{loanAmount}} × {{pmiPct}}% ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month. PMI typically lasts until you reach 20% equity (then auto-drops on conventional loans per Homeowners Protection Act).

promptTemplate: You want to buy a ${{purchasePrice}} home with {{downPct}}% down at a 6% rate (factor 0.006). Assuming ~1.5%/yr tax + insurance, what minimum GROSS monthly income do you need (28% rule)?
explanationTemplate: Loan = price × (1 − down%). P&I = loan × rate factor. PITI ≈ P&I + (price × 1.5% ÷ 12). Min income = PITI ÷ 0.28. The full chain gives ${{answer}}/month gross income needed.

promptTemplate: Gross monthly income $7,000. At a 6.5% rate (factor ~0.00632), 10% down, ~$300/mo expected tax+insurance, ignoring PMI for simplicity — roughly what's your max purchase price?
explanationTemplate: Max PITI = $7,000 × 28% = $1,960. P&I after tax+ins = $1,960 − $300 = $1,660. Max loan = $1,660 ÷ 0.00632 ≈ $263k. With 10% down: max price = $263k ÷ 0.9 ≈ $292k. (PMI on the 90% loan would shave another ~$100/mo off the loan headroom — most buyers under 20% down end up about 5-10% below this number.)
conceptChoices: About $450k — affordable on $7k/mo gross
About $290k — using the 28% rule, tax+ins haircut, and rate factor
About $200k — being conservative
About $370k — using 32% instead of 28%
correctConceptChoice: About $290k — using the 28% rule, tax+ins haircut, and rate factor

promptTemplate: Your ${{currentRent}}/month rent is going up by {{increasePercent}}%. The national average is 4%. By how much MORE per month are you paying vs the average increase?
explanationTemplate: Above-average = rent × (increase − 4%) ÷ 100 = ${{answer}}/month above what an average renewal would cost.

promptTemplate: Your landlord raises rent by ${{monthlyIncrease}}/month. Moving to a similar place costs ${{movingCost}} (broker + deposits + movers). How many months until staying costs more than moving?
explanationTemplate: Months to break even = moving cost ÷ monthly increase = ${{movingCost}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncrease}} = ~{{answer}} months. Lease shorter than that? Stay.

promptTemplate: ${{loanAmount}} mortgage at 6% over 30 years uses factor 0.006. Estimate the monthly payment.
explanationTemplate: Monthly = loan × factor. ${{loanAmount}} × 0.006 = ${{answer}}. Accurate within $5 of actual amortization.

promptTemplate: At 6% over 30 years, each $100k of mortgage costs about $600/month. What's the monthly payment on a ${{loanAmount}} loan?
explanationTemplate: $600 per $100k. ${{loanAmount}} ÷ $100k × $600 = ${{answer}}/mo.

promptTemplate: ${{loanAmount}} mortgage. At 5% the factor is 0.0054; at 7% it's 0.0067. How much more per month does the 7% rate cost?
explanationTemplate: Diff = loan × (0.0067 − 0.0054) = loan × 0.0013. ${{loanAmount}} × 0.0013 = ${{answer}}/mo more at 7%.

promptTemplate: ${{loanAmount}} mortgage at 6% (factor 0.006) plus ${{taxAndInsurance}}/month for property tax + insurance. What's your total monthly housing cost?
explanationTemplate: P&I = loan × 0.006. Total = P&I + tax/ins = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Renting: ${{monthlyRent}}/month. Buying: ${{loanAmount}} mortgage at 6% (factor 0.006) + ${{taxAndInsurance}}/month for tax/insurance. Which is cheaper per month, and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Mortgage total = loan × 0.006 + tax/ins. Difference vs rent = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: A 2BR apartment rents for ${{sharedRent}}/month. Split evenly with a roommate, what do you pay?
explanationTemplate: ${{sharedRent}} ÷ 2 = ${{answer}}/month per person.

promptTemplate: Living alone in a 1BR: ${{soloRent}}/month + ${{soloUtilities}} utilities. Sharing a 2BR: ${{sharedRent}}/month + ${{sharedUtilities}} utilities split with a roommate. How much do you save monthly with a roommate?
explanationTemplate: Solo total − (shared total ÷ 2). (${{soloRent}} + ${{soloUtilities}}) − ((${{sharedRent}} + ${{sharedUtilities}}) ÷ 2) = ${{answer}}/mo savings.

promptTemplate: A 2BR is ${{sharedRent}}/month. The bigger bedroom takes {{bigShare}}% of the rent. What does the smaller-bedroom roommate pay?
explanationTemplate: Smaller-bedroom share = (100 − {{bigShare}})% × ${{sharedRent}} = ${{answer}}/mo.

promptTemplate: You save ${{monthlySaving}}/month by having a roommate. How much do you save per year?
explanationTemplate: Monthly × 12. ${{monthlySaving}} × 12 = ${{answer}}/year.

promptTemplate: Solo 1BR: ${{soloRent}}/mo. Shared 2BR: ${{sharedRent}}/mo (your half: half of that). What's your annual savings?
explanationTemplate: Monthly saving = solo − (shared ÷ 2). × 12 = ${{answer}}/year.

promptTemplate: Monthly housing: rent ${{rent}}, utilities ${{utilities}}, insurance ${{insurance}}, parking ${{parking}}. What's your TRUE monthly housing cost?
explanationTemplate: Add them all. ${{rent}} + ${{utilities}} + ${{insurance}} + ${{parking}} = ${{answer}}/month true cost.

promptTemplate: Your true monthly housing cost is ${{trueCost}}. Your rent alone is ${{rent}}. How much MORE per month is the true cost above just rent?
explanationTemplate: True cost − rent = hidden housing costs. ${{trueCost}} − ${{rent}} = ${{answer}}/mo.

promptTemplate: Apartment A: rent ${{rentA}}, total housing add-ons ${{addonsA}}. Apartment B: rent ${{rentB}}, add-ons ${{addonsB}}. Which has the lower TRUE monthly cost, and by how much?
explanationTemplate: A total = ${{rentA}}+${{addonsA}}. B total = ${{rentB}}+${{addonsB}}. Difference = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Rent is ${{rent}}/month. True total housing cost is ${{trueCost}}. What percentage is the 'extra' above rent?
explanationTemplate: Extra / rent × 100. (${{trueCost}} − ${{rent}}) ÷ ${{rent}} × 100 = {{answer}}%.

promptTemplate: Monthly income ${{monthlyIncome}}. Your TRUE housing cost (rent + utilities + insurance + parking) is ${{trueCost}}. What percentage of income is housing eating?
explanationTemplate: True cost ÷ income × 100. ${{trueCost}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = {{answer}}%. Above 28%? Budget-stressed.

promptTemplate: Your lease has an early termination fee of {{monthsPenalty}} months' rent. Rent is ${{monthlyRent}}. What's the break fee?
explanationTemplate: {{monthsPenalty}} × ${{monthlyRent}} = ${{answer}} fee.

promptTemplate: Lease break fee = {{monthsPenalty}} months × ${{monthlyRent}}. Moving costs ${{movingCost}}. Total cost to break?
explanationTemplate: (months × rent) + moving = ${{answer}} total break cost.

promptTemplate: Total cost to break: ${{totalBreakCost}}. You'd save ${{monthlySaving}}/month at the new place. How many months until savings exceed break cost?
explanationTemplate: Break-even = break cost ÷ monthly saving = ${{totalBreakCost}} ÷ ${{monthlySaving}} = {{answer}} months.

promptTemplate: Lease has {{monthsLeft}} months remaining. Breaking costs ${{totalBreakCost}}. New place saves ${{monthlySaving}}/month. By staying, how much MORE money do you keep vs breaking?
explanationTemplate: Stay: pay $0 break, lose monthsLeft × saving in foregone savings. Break: pay break cost, gain monthsLeft × saving. Net: ${{answer}} more by staying when break > savings.

promptTemplate: {{monthsLeft}} months left at ${{currentRent}}/month. New apartment: ${{newRent}}/month. Breaking costs ${{breakFee}} in penalty + ${{movingCost}} to move. Net cost to break (break costs − savings from cheaper rent for remaining months)?
explanationTemplate: Net cost = (breakFee + moving) − (monthsLeft × (currentRent − newRent)). Positive = staying is cheaper. = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You got a ${{refundAmount}} tax refund this year. That means you over-withheld each month. How much extra per month was the IRS holding (interest-free)?
explanationTemplate: Refund ÷ 12. ${{refundAmount}} ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month extra you could've kept.

promptTemplate: You got a ${{refundAmount}} refund. If you'd reduced withholding and invested the extra at 6% (~half-year avg return), how much would you have GAINED beyond the refund?
explanationTemplate: Approx gain ≈ refund × 3%. ${{refundAmount}} × 3% = ${{answer}} forfeited in lost growth.

promptTemplate: Your employer withholds ${{monthlyWithheld}}/month. Your actual monthly tax burden is ${{monthlyOwed}}. What's your annual over-withholding (= refund you'll get)?
explanationTemplate: (withheld − owed) × 12 = ${{answer}}. That's your interest-free loan to the IRS.

promptTemplate: You earned ${{quarterlyIncome}} freelancing this quarter. SE tax (15.3% on 92.35% of earnings) + income tax ~{{incomeTaxPct}}%. What's your quarterly estimated payment?
explanationTemplate: SE: ${{quarterlyIncome}} × 92.35% × 15.3%. + income: ${{quarterlyIncome}} × {{incomeTaxPct}}%. Total ≈ ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Mortgage interest ${{mortgageInt}}, state/local taxes ${{stateTax}}, charitable donations ${{charity}}. What's your total itemized deduction?
explanationTemplate: Add them: ${{mortgageInt}} + ${{stateTax}} + ${{charity}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Your itemized total is ${{itemizedAmount}}. Standard deduction is ${{standardAmount}}. By how much does itemizing exceed standard?
explanationTemplate: ${{itemizedAmount}} − ${{standardAmount}} = ${{answer}} above standard.

promptTemplate: Your itemized exceeds standard by ${{excessAmount}}. At a {{taxRate}}% marginal rate, how much extra tax saving does itemizing give you?
explanationTemplate: Excess × tax rate. ${{excessAmount}} × {{taxRate}}% = ${{answer}} extra in refund.

promptTemplate: Mortgage interest ${{mortgageInt}} + state tax ${{stateTax}} + charity ${{charity}}. Standard deduction is $16,100. At {{taxRate}}% bracket, how much extra do you save by itemizing?
explanationTemplate: Itemized total − $16,100 = excess. Excess × tax rate = ${{answer}}. If negative, take standard.

promptTemplate: You itemize and save ${{annualSaving}} more than standard. Over a {{years}}-year career of homeownership, what's the cumulative tax saving?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualSaving}} × {{years}} = ${{answer}} cumulative. Worth the extra paperwork at tax time.

promptTemplate: You made a ${{gain}} gain on a stock held for {{months}} months (short-term). At {{ordinaryRate}}% ordinary tax rate, what's the tax?
explanationTemplate: Short-term = ordinary rate. ${{gain}} × {{ordinaryRate}}% = ${{answer}} tax.

promptTemplate: You made a ${{gain}} gain on a stock held over 1 year. At {{ltcgRate}}% long-term capital gains rate, what's the tax?
explanationTemplate: Long-term = special rate. ${{gain}} × {{ltcgRate}}% = ${{answer}} tax.

promptTemplate: ${{gain}} gain. Short-term rate {{ordinaryRate}}%. Long-term rate {{ltcgRate}}%. How much do you save by waiting past 1 year?
explanationTemplate: Saving = gain × (ordinary − ltcg). ${{gain}} × ({{ordinaryRate}}% − {{ltcgRate}}%) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You've held a stock for 11 months. ${{gain}} unrealized gain. Sell now (short-term {{ordinaryRate}}%) vs wait 1 more month (long-term {{ltcgRate}}%) — how much do you save by waiting?
explanationTemplate: ${{gain}} × ({{ordinaryRate}}% − {{ltcgRate}}%) = ${{answer}}. One month of patience pays.

promptTemplate: Investor A: holds {{shortMonths}} months, ${{gainA}} gain at {{ordinaryRate}}%. Investor B: holds 13 months, ${{gainB}} gain at {{ltcgRate}}%. Whose tax bill is lower, and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Tax A = gainA × ordinary. Tax B = gainB × ltcg. Difference = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Last year's refund: ${{refundAmount}}. You're paid monthly. How much more should you keep per paycheck by adjusting your W-4?
explanationTemplate: Refund ÷ 12. ${{refundAmount}} ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/check more.

promptTemplate: Last year's refund: ${{refundAmount}}. You're paid biweekly (26 paychecks). How much per check by adjusting W-4?
explanationTemplate: Refund ÷ 26. ${{refundAmount}} ÷ 26 = ${{answer}}/biweekly check.

promptTemplate: You bump each biweekly paycheck by ${{biweeklyBump}} and invest it at 6%/year. Approximate end-of-year balance? (use simple 3% half-year avg return)
explanationTemplate: Total contributed × 1.03 ≈ end value. (${{biweeklyBump}} × 26) × 1.03 = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You'd otherwise get a ${{refundAmount}} refund. Instead, you adjust your W-4, invest the extra at 6%/year. Approximate end-of-year gain BEYOND the refund?
explanationTemplate: Approx gain ≈ refund × 3% = ${{answer}} extra by investing instead of waiting.

promptTemplate: If you over-withhold ${{refundAmount}} every year for {{years}} years and invest at 6% annually instead, your approximate gain (vs taking refunds): refund × 3% × years compounding. Simplified: refund × 0.03 × years = ?
explanationTemplate: ${{refundAmount}} × 3% × {{years}} = ${{answer}} approximate lifetime forfeit.

promptTemplate: Health plan: ${{monthlyPremium}}/month premium, ${{deductible}} deductible. What's your exposure range (worst-case − best-case annual cost)?
explanationTemplate: Range = deductible (the gap between best and worst case). Higher deductible = more exposure if you have a bad year. ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: ER visit: ${{totalBill}} total. Your deductible is ${{deductible}} (already paid ${{deductibleSoFar}} this year). Coinsurance is {{coinsurancePercent}}%. How much do you pay out of pocket for this visit?
explanationTemplate: Pay remaining deductible + coinsurance on rest. (${{deductible}} − ${{deductibleSoFar}}) + (${{totalBill}} − ${{deductible}}) × {{coinsurancePercent}}% = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Doctor visit costs ${{visitCost}}. Plan A: ${{copayAmount}} copay. Plan B: {{coinsurancePercent}}% coinsurance (deductible already met). Which costs less for THIS visit, and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Copay = ${{copayAmount}}. Coinsurance = ${{visitCost}} × {{coinsurancePercent}}%. Difference = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: HDHP: ${{hdhpPremium}}/mo, ${{hdhpVisitCost}}/visit until deductible met. PPO: ${{ppoPremium}}/mo, ${{ppoCopay}}/visit. Monthly premium savings on HDHP × 12 = annual savings. How many doctor visits would make the PPO cheaper than HDHP?
explanationTemplate: Annual premium saving on HDHP = (PPO − HDHP) × 12. Per visit, HDHP costs (HDHP visit − PPO copay) more. Break-even visits ≈ saving ÷ per-visit gap = {{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{hsaAnnual}}/year to HSA from age 30 to 65. At 7% growth, balance ≈ ${{projectedBalance}}. If you withdraw ${{medicalAmount}} in retirement for medical, how much tax do you save vs a Traditional IRA at {{taxRate}}%?
explanationTemplate: Medical withdrawal from HSA = $0 tax. Same withdrawal from Traditional = withdrawal × tax rate = ${{answer}} saved.

promptTemplate: You elect ${{fsaElection}} to your FSA. Your tax rate is {{taxRate}}%. How much do you save in taxes?
explanationTemplate: Tax saved = election × tax rate. ${{fsaElection}} × {{taxRate}}% = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: FSA election: ${{fsaElection}}. Tax rate: {{taxRate}}%. You actually spend ${{actualSpent}} on medical. What's your NET financial result (tax savings minus forfeited unspent funds)?
explanationTemplate: Tax saved − unspent forfeit. (${{fsaElection}} × {{taxRate}}%) − (${{fsaElection}} − ${{actualSpent}}) = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: FSA election ${{fsaElection}} at {{taxRate}}% tax bracket. What's the MINIMUM you must spend on medical to break even (not lose money)?
explanationTemplate: Break-even = election × (1 − tax rate). ${{fsaElection}} × (1 − {{taxRate}}%) = ${{answer}}. Spend less than this and you lose money.

promptTemplate: FSA Option A: elect ${{electionA}}. Option B: elect ${{electionB}}. At {{taxRate}}% tax rate, what's the maximum extra tax saving from electing the higher amount?
explanationTemplate: (Higher − lower) × tax rate. (${{electionB}} − ${{electionA}}) × {{taxRate}}% = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: You'll definitely spend ${{guaranteedSpend}} on medical this year. At {{taxRate}}% bracket, how much MORE could you safely elect to FSA? (Hint: max election where you still break even.)
explanationTemplate: Max safe extra = guaranteedSpend × (tax/(1−tax)). Anything extra above this loses money if unspent. ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Annual salary ${{annualSalary}}. Using the 10× rule, what's your baseline life insurance need?
explanationTemplate: Salary × 10. ${{annualSalary}} × 10 = ${{answer}} baseline coverage.

promptTemplate: Salary ${{annualSalary}} (use 10× rule). Mortgage balance ${{mortgageBalance}}. Savings ${{savings}}. What's your adjusted life insurance need?
explanationTemplate: (salary × 10) + mortgage − savings = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Quote A: ${{premiumA}}/month for ${{coverageA}} coverage. Quote B: ${{premiumB}}/month for ${{coverageB}} coverage. How much MORE does Quote B cost annually?
explanationTemplate: (premiumB − premiumA) × 12. (${{premiumB}} − ${{premiumA}}) × 12 = ${{answer}}/yr extra for B.

promptTemplate: A 30-year term policy: ${{coverage}} coverage, ${{premium}}/month premium. What's the annual cost per $100,000 of coverage?
explanationTemplate: Annual premium ÷ (coverage / $100k). (${{premium}} × 12) ÷ ({{coverage}} / 100k) = ${{answer}} per $100k/yr.

promptTemplate: You'll pay ${{monthlyPremium}}/month for a 30-year term policy. What's the total cost over the policy lifetime?
explanationTemplate: Monthly × 12 × 30. ${{monthlyPremium}} × 360 = ${{answer}} over 30 years (vs term cost of whole life: typically 10-15× more).

promptTemplate: Brand copay: ${{brandCopay}}. Generic copay: ${{genericCopay}}. With 12 monthly refills, what's your annual saving by switching to generic?
explanationTemplate: (brand − generic) × 12. (${{brandCopay}} − ${{genericCopay}}) × 12 = ${{answer}}/yr saved.

promptTemplate: You take two brand-name drugs with copays of ${{copay1}} and ${{copay2}}. The generics cost ${{generic1}} and ${{generic2}}. Combined annual saving if you switch both?
explanationTemplate: ((${{copay1}} − ${{generic1}}) + (${{copay2}} − ${{generic2}})) × 12 = ${{answer}}/yr.

promptTemplate: Brand with insurance: ${{brandCopay}}/month copay. Generic via GoodRx (no insurance): ${{goodrxPrice}}/month cash. Annual savings going GoodRx route?
explanationTemplate: Sometimes cash price is cheaper than insurance. (${{brandCopay}} − ${{goodrxPrice}}) × 12 = ${{answer}}/yr.

promptTemplate: Brand copay ${{brandCopay}}, generic copay ${{genericCopay}}. What's the monthly difference?
explanationTemplate: ${{brandCopay}} − ${{genericCopay}} = ${{answer}}/month saved.

promptTemplate: You save ${{monthlyDiff}}/month switching one prescription to generic. Over {{years}} years, total saved?
explanationTemplate: ${{monthlyDiff}} × 12 × {{years}} = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Same ${{loanAmount}} car loan. 48-month payment: ${{payment48}}/month. 72-month payment: ${{payment72}}/month. By choosing 72 months, your monthly drops but TOTAL cost rises by how much?
explanationTemplate: (72 × p72) − (48 × p48) = ${{answer}} extra paid for the lower monthly. Dealer's profit, your loss.

promptTemplate: $30,000 car at 7% over 60 months. With ${{downPayment}} down, total interest is approximately ${{totalInterest}}. With ${{higherDown}} down instead, interest drops to ${{lowerInterest}}. How much do you save by putting more down?
explanationTemplate: ${{totalInterest}} − ${{lowerInterest}} = ${{answer}} interest saved by larger down payment.

promptTemplate: New ${{carPrice}} car. Depreciates {{depPercent}}% over 3 years. Plus ${{monthlyOps}}/month for insurance + gas. What's your TOTAL 3-year cost of ownership (depreciation + ops)?
explanationTemplate: Depreciation = price × dep%. Ops = monthly × 36. Total = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Monthly car costs: payment ${{payment}}, insurance ${{insurance}}, gas ${{gas}}, maintenance ${{maintenance}}. Total monthly ownership cost?
explanationTemplate: Sum it all. ${{payment}} + ${{insurance}} + ${{gas}} + ${{maintenance}} = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Car A: ${{paymentA}}/mo payment, ${{opsA}}/mo other costs. Car B: ${{paymentB}}/mo payment, ${{opsB}}/mo other costs. Which has lower monthly TCO and by how much?
explanationTemplate: A total = paymentA + opsA. B total = paymentB + opsB. Difference = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Keep current paid-off car: ${{maintenanceKeep}}/mo maintenance + ${{insuranceKeep}}/mo insurance + ${{gasKeep}}/mo gas. Buy new: ${{paymentNew}}/mo payment + ${{opsNew}}/mo all other costs. How much more does buying cost per month?
explanationTemplate: Buy total − keep total = monthly cost of buying new. ${{answer}}/month is what you'd save by keeping.

promptTemplate: Monthly income ${{monthlyIncome}}. Total monthly car cost: ${{tcoMonthly}}. What % of income is your car eating?
explanationTemplate: TCO ÷ income × 100. ${{tcoMonthly}} ÷ ${{monthlyIncome}} × 100 = {{answer}}%. Above 10%? Car-poor.

promptTemplate: Your monthly TCO is ${{tcoMonthly}}. What's your annual car cost?
explanationTemplate: Monthly × 12. ${{tcoMonthly}} × 12 = ${{answer}}/year.

promptTemplate: Lease: ${{monthlyLease}}/month for {{months}} months. Total spent at end?
explanationTemplate: Monthly × months. ${{monthlyLease}} × {{months}} = ${{answer}} total (and you own nothing).

promptTemplate: Buy: ${{monthlyPayment}}/mo × {{months}} months. After {{months}} months the car is worth ${{residualValue}}. What's your NET cost of ownership?
explanationTemplate: Net = (payment × months) − residual value. You spent money but built equity. = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Lease ${{monthlyLease}}/mo × 36 months. Or buy ${{monthlyPayment}}/mo × 36 months; car worth ${{residualValue}} at month 36. Which is cheaper over 3 years and by how much?
explanationTemplate: Lease cost: monthly × 36. Buy net: (payment × 36) − residual. Diff = ${{answer}}. Buying almost always wins if you keep the car.

promptTemplate: 3-year lease total spent: ${{leaseTotal}}. What was the monthly lease payment?
explanationTemplate: Total ÷ 36 months. ${{leaseTotal}} ÷ 36 = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: Over 10 years: lease 3 cars at ${{leasePerCar}} each (over 3 years each, 9 years coverage). Or buy 1 car ${{carPrice}}, drive 10 years (no payments after year 5). Approximate 10-yr difference?
explanationTemplate: Lease total ≈ leasePerCar × 3.33 (rolling leases). Buy ≈ carPrice. Difference = ${{answer}} more for leasing.

promptTemplate: Dealer trade-in offer: ${{tradeInOffer}}. Private sale market value: ${{privatePrice}}. What's the convenience premium you give up to the dealer?
explanationTemplate: Private − trade-in = ${{answer}} convenience cost.

promptTemplate: Selling privately would gain you ${{premium}} more than trading in. Estimated hours of effort: {{hours}}. What's your effective hourly rate for selling yourself?
explanationTemplate: Premium ÷ hours. ${{premium}} ÷ {{hours}} = ${{answer}}/hour effective wage.

promptTemplate: In your state, trading in reduces the sales tax base on the new car. Trade-in value: ${{tradeInOffer}}. Sales tax rate: {{taxRate}}%. How much sales tax does the trade-in save you?
explanationTemplate: Trade-in × tax rate. ${{tradeInOffer}} × {{taxRate}}% = ${{answer}} sales tax saved.

promptTemplate: Private sale would net ${{privatePrice}}. Trade-in is ${{tradeInOffer}}. The trade-in saves you ${{taxSaving}} in sales tax. What's the ADJUSTED premium for selling privately?
explanationTemplate: (Private − trade-in) − tax saving = ${{answer}} real premium after accounting for tax benefit.

promptTemplate: Private sale: ${{privatePrice}}. Trade-in: ${{tradeInOffer}} + ${{taxSaving}} sales tax saved. Estimated hours to sell privately: {{hours}}. What's the effective hourly rate for going private (after tax savings)?
explanationTemplate: Adjusted premium ÷ hours = effective hourly = ${{answer}}/hour. Above $50/hr makes private selling worth it for most people.

promptTemplate: Standard 10-year repayment: ~$110 per $10,000 borrowed at 5% APR. Your balance is ${{loanBalance}}. Estimate your monthly payment.
explanationTemplate: Balance ÷ $10k × $110. ${{loanBalance}} ÷ 10k × $110 = ${{answer}}/month.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. Rule of thumb says ~${{paymentPer10k}} per $10k at this APR. Estimated monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: (Balance ÷ 10k) × ${{paymentPer10k}}. ${{loanBalance}} → ${{answer}}/mo.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. Lower-rate estimate: $100/$10k. Higher-rate estimate: $120/$10k. What's the monthly payment RANGE (difference between high and low estimate)?
explanationTemplate: Balance ÷ 10k × ($120 − $100) = $20 per $10k. ${{loanBalance}} → ${{answer}} range between low and high rate estimates.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan at ~{{apr}}% APR. Using $100/$10k for 4-5% and $120/$10k for 6-7%, what's your estimated monthly payment?
explanationTemplate: APR 4-5%: × $105. APR 6-7%: × $115. Balance/10k × rate-appropriate factor = ${{answer}}/mo.

promptTemplate: You borrowed ${{loanAmount}}. Total you'll repay: ${{totalPaid}}. What percentage of the original loan are you paying in interest?
explanationTemplate: (totalPaid − loan) ÷ loan × 100. (${{totalPaid}} − ${{loanAmount}}) ÷ ${{loanAmount}} × 100 = {{answer}}%.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. Refi option: ${{refiPayment}}/mo × 120 mo. PSLF option: ${{pslfPayment}}/mo × 120 mo (rest forgiven). How much more does refinancing cost vs PSLF?
explanationTemplate: (refi − pslf) × 120 months = ${{answer}} more for refinancing. But: PSLF requires public service for 10 years.

promptTemplate: Your employer contributes ${{annualBenefit}}/year toward your student loans (tax-free). What's the monthly equivalent going to your principal?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualBenefit}} ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month direct to your principal.

promptTemplate: Employer contributes ${{annualBenefit}}/year. Over {{years}} years of employment, total benefit?
explanationTemplate: ${{annualBenefit}} × {{years}} = ${{answer}} total employer-paid principal.

promptTemplate: Employer pays ${{annualBenefit}}/year × {{years}} years toward a ${{loanBalance}} loan at {{interestRate}}% interest. Approximate additional interest saved (rough: benefit × rate × years / 2)?
explanationTemplate: Rough: benefit × years × rate × 0.5 (half years of avoided interest). = ${{answer}}.

promptTemplate: Employer offers ${{annualBenefit}}/yr tax-free student loan match. At your {{taxRate}}% tax rate, what's the equivalent pre-tax salary raise (gross-up)?
explanationTemplate: Benefit ÷ (1 − tax rate). ${{annualBenefit}} ÷ (1 − {{taxRate}}%) = ${{answer}} equivalent pre-tax raise.

promptTemplate: If you stay at the employer for {{years}} years receiving full ${{annualBenefit}}/yr benefit, and that money would otherwise have to come from after-tax pay at {{taxRate}}%, what's the total pre-tax-equivalent value?
explanationTemplate: (benefit ÷ (1 − tax rate)) × years = ${{answer}} total equivalent salary value.

promptTemplate: Your unsubsidized loan balance is ${{balance}} at {{interestRate}}% APR. What's the daily interest accruing?
explanationTemplate: Balance × rate ÷ 365. ${{balance}} × {{interestRate}}% ÷ 365 = ${{answer}}/day accruing.

promptTemplate: Daily interest on your loan is ${{dailyAmount}}. Over the 180-day grace period, how much interest accrues?
explanationTemplate: ${{dailyAmount}} × 180 = ${{answer}} added to your principal at grace end.

promptTemplate: ${{balance}} loan at {{interestRate}}% APR. If you skip grace-period payments, ${{accruedAmount}} interest capitalizes. If you make interest-only payments instead, you save the capitalized amount + future interest on it. Approximate total saving (capitalized + ~5% of capitalized for future interest)?
explanationTemplate: Saving ≈ accrued × 1.05 = ${{answer}}. Interest-only during grace prevents capitalization.

promptTemplate: Your loan was ${{originalBalance}} when you graduated. After 6 months of grace with interest accruing at {{interestRate}}% APR, what's the new balance at repayment start?
explanationTemplate: Original + (balance × rate × 0.5). New balance = ${{answer}} at start of repayment.

promptTemplate: If grace-period interest of ${{accruedAmount}} capitalizes onto your ${{balance}} loan at {{interestRate}}% APR, approximately how much extra interest do you pay over a 10-year repayment (rough: capitalized × rate × 5)?
explanationTemplate: Extra ≈ capitalized × rate × 5 years avg. = ${{answer}} over loan life.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. Parent PLUS rate {{plusRate}}%. Private alternative {{privateRate}}%. What's the annual interest difference?
explanationTemplate: Balance × (plus − private) ÷ 100 = ${{answer}}/year more on PLUS.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. Parent PLUS at {{plusRate}}% vs private at {{privateRate}}%. Approximate 10-year interest difference (annual diff × 10, simplified)?
explanationTemplate: Balance × (plus − private) × 10 ÷ 100 = ${{answer}} over 10 years (simplified).

promptTemplate: Parent PLUS loans have a 4.228% origination fee deducted upfront. On a ${{loanBalance}} loan, how much is the origination fee?
explanationTemplate: Balance × 4.228%. ${{loanBalance}} × 4.228% = ${{answer}} taken off the top before you receive funds.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} Parent PLUS at 9.07% + 4.228% origination. Private alternative: {{privateRate}}% no fee. Approximate total 10-yr difference (interest gap × 10 + origination)?
explanationTemplate: (balance × (9.07 − private) × 10 + balance × 4.228) ÷ 100 = ${{answer}} private advantage.

promptTemplate: ${{loanBalance}} loan. PLUS annual interest at 9.07% vs private at {{privateRate}}%. Annual interest savings = balance × rate difference. How much more per month does PLUS cost you in interest?
explanationTemplate: Annual diff ÷ 12. Balance × (9.07 − private) ÷ 100 ÷ 12 = ${{answer}}/month more on PLUS.

promptTemplate: What is 'anchoring' in retail pricing?
explanationTemplate: Anchoring exploits the contrast between a high reference price and a 'sale' price. The original price doesn't need to be one anyone actually paid — its job is to make the current price feel like a deal.
conceptChoices: Showing a high original price (often inflated) alongside a sale price to make the discount feel bigger
Charging different prices to different customers based on their location
Offering different prices on different days of the week
The practice of rounding prices up to the nearest dollar
correctConceptChoice: Showing a high original price (often inflated) alongside a sale price to make the discount feel bigger

promptTemplate: A movie theater offers small popcorn $4, medium $7, large $7.50. Which is the 'decoy' pricing tactic?
explanationTemplate: The medium is the decoy: priced just below the large so the large feels like a steal. Without the medium, you'd compare $4 vs $7.50 and likely pick the small. This is one of the most common pricing tactics in retail.
conceptChoices: Small — it's underpriced to lure you in
Medium — it makes the large look like a great deal at only $0.50 more
Large — it's overpriced to anchor on expense
There's no decoy here — these are standard prices
correctConceptChoice: Medium — it makes the large look like a great deal at only $0.50 more

promptTemplate: Why do stores price items at $9.99 instead of $10.00?
explanationTemplate: Charm pricing (.99 endings) exploits 'left-digit bias' — your brain reads $9.99 and registers '$9-something' rather than '$10'. Studies show this boosts conversions despite the trivial price difference.
conceptChoices: Most shoppers anchor on the first digit, so $9 feels much less than $10 — even though the difference is one cent
It's actually 10% cheaper because of the missing dollar
It triggers an automatic discount at checkout
It's required by retail tax law
correctConceptChoice: Most shoppers anchor on the first digit, so $9 feels much less than $10 — even though the difference is one cent

promptTemplate: A retailer's tag reads: 'Original $200, now $129!' Which is most likely true about the 'original' price?
explanationTemplate: MSRPs are set by manufacturers as a reference, not as a real-world price. Most stores discount permanently from MSRP — the 'sale price' IS the regular price. Comparing to competitor pricing tells you the real value.
conceptChoices: The 'original $200' is the manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) which nobody actually pays — $129 is closer to the real market price
The store is losing $71 on the sale and hoping to make it up on other items
The $200 was the price last week, before the sale started
The discount is fraud — illegal in most US states
correctConceptChoice: The 'original $200' is the manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) which nobody actually pays — $129 is closer to the real market price

promptTemplate: A grocer normally sells chicken wings for $11.99/lb. During a BOGO Free promotion, the 'regular price' is listed as $19.99/lb. What's actually happening?
explanationTemplate: This exact tactic was the subject of multiple 2024 grocery lawsuits. Inflating the 'regular price' during a BOGO turns the 'free' item into a fiction. Compare to recent prices you've actually paid — not the in-promotion 'regular' price.
conceptChoices: The 'regular price' was inflated for the promotion so the 'free' pound is illusory — you're effectively paying $9.99/lb for two pounds
The store is charging $7.99 extra for the convenience of the deal
The deal is a typo on the price tag — should be honored at $11.99
Chicken prices doubled the week of the promotion
correctConceptChoice: The 'regular price' was inflated for the promotion so the 'free' pound is illusory — you're effectively paying $9.99/lb for two pounds

promptTemplate: Under the 50/30/20 rule, what counts as a 'need'?
explanationTemplate: 'Needs' under 50/30/20 means survival/non-negotiable: shelter, basic food, utilities, insurance, transportation to work, and minimum debt payments. Subscriptions, gym, dining out — those are wants no matter how routine they feel.
conceptChoices: Anything you spend money on regularly (subscriptions, gym, takeout)
Expenses you'd struggle to live without — rent, basic groceries, utilities, insurance, work transport, debt minimums
Only housing and food
Anything under $50
correctConceptChoice: Expenses you'd struggle to live without — rent, basic groceries, utilities, insurance, work transport, debt minimums

promptTemplate: You go to the gym 4× a week, $40/month. In a 50/30/20 budget, this is a...
explanationTemplate: Gym membership is a want, no matter how committed you are. The litmus test: if you lost your job tomorrow, would you cancel it immediately? Yes → want. Real needs (rent, insurance) can't be canceled.
conceptChoices: Need — health is a basic necessity
Want — important for wellbeing but not survival-critical
Need if you'd otherwise have higher healthcare costs
Depends on whether you use it daily
correctConceptChoice: Want — important for wellbeing but not survival-critical

promptTemplate: A $15/month Netflix subscription. In a 50/30/20 budget, this counts as a...
explanationTemplate: All entertainment subscriptions are wants. The 30% 'wants' bucket exists specifically for this — guilt-free spending on things that make life enjoyable, as long as they fit within 30% of take-home.
conceptChoices: Need (entertainment is necessary for mental health)
Want (entertainment is rarely a need)
Savings (replaces other paid entertainment)
Depends on whether you have kids
correctConceptChoice: Want (entertainment is rarely a need)

promptTemplate: Your needs total 62% of take-home pay (rent alone is 40%). What does 50/30/20 say you should do?
explanationTemplate: When needs exceed 50%, the framework is broken until something gives. Either accept lower wants + savings (often unsustainable), or address the structural issue — usually housing. Roommates, smaller place, cheaper city.
conceptChoices: Just stop saving — increase your spending elsewhere
Move savings to a higher-yield account to make up for it
Cut wants/savings to fit, OR reduce housing costs (cheaper place, roommate)
Borrow against next month to balance it out
correctConceptChoice: Cut wants/savings to fit, OR reduce housing costs (cheaper place, roommate)

promptTemplate: You lose your job tomorrow. Which expense moves from 'want' to a higher priority (effectively a need)?
explanationTemplate: When you lose employer health coverage, insurance shifts from 'employer perk' to a critical need you must buy yourself. COBRA, marketplace plans, or a partner's plan become essential — this is why the emergency fund matters.
conceptChoices: Streaming subscriptions — you'll have more free time
Gym membership — exercise is even more important
Health insurance — it's now critical to buy on your own (COBRA or marketplace)
Your daily latte — it's a small comfort during a hard time
correctConceptChoice: Health insurance — it's now critical to buy on your own (COBRA or marketplace)

promptTemplate: Under the FLSA, an 'exempt' employee is...
explanationTemplate: 'Exempt' means exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime rules. You're paid a fixed salary regardless of how many hours you work — could be 35 or 65 a week, same paycheck.
conceptChoices: Exempt from overtime pay rules — they earn a fixed salary regardless of hours worked
Exempt from federal income tax
Exempt from working more than 40 hours per week
Exempt from employer-provided benefits
correctConceptChoice: Exempt from overtime pay rules — they earn a fixed salary regardless of hours worked

promptTemplate: Under the FLSA, a 'non-exempt' employee must be paid...
explanationTemplate: Non-exempt employees are entitled to overtime pay at 1.5× their regular rate for hours beyond 40 in a workweek. This applies regardless of job title — what matters is the legal classification.
conceptChoices: At least minimum wage but no overtime
Overtime (1.5×) for any hours worked beyond 40 per week
The same as exempt employees with a tax deduction
Quarterly bonuses regardless of performance
correctConceptChoice: Overtime (1.5×) for any hours worked beyond 40 per week

promptTemplate: After a Texas federal court vacated the 2024 DOL overtime rule in November 2024, what's the currently enforced federal minimum salary for FLSA-exempt status?
explanationTemplate: The federal threshold reverted to $35,568/year ($684/week — the 2019 level) after the November 2024 Texas court ruling vacated the DOL's $58,656 increase. Many states have set higher thresholds — California is around $66,560, New York and Washington are also higher. Always check both federal and state law.
conceptChoices: $35,568/year (reverted federal threshold after Nov 2024 court ruling)
$58,656/year (the vacated 2024 DOL rule)
correctConceptChoice: $35,568/year (reverted federal threshold after Nov 2024 court ruling)

promptTemplate: An admin assistant earns $45,000/year and is labeled 'exempt' (no overtime). Is this likely legal?
explanationTemplate: Misclassification is common. To be exempt federally, an employee must (1) earn at least $35,568/year (the current federal floor after the Nov 2024 court ruling) AND (2) perform exempt duties (executive, administrative, professional). State thresholds are often higher — California's is around $66,560. Admin assistants usually fail the duties test. At $45k with no genuine executive duties, this is likely misclassification — you may be owed back overtime pay.
conceptChoices: Yes — employers can classify any employee as exempt
Yes — admin staff are always exempt
No — below the federal salary threshold AND admin work typically fails the 'duties test' for exemption
It depends entirely on which state they work in
correctConceptChoice: No — below the federal salary threshold AND admin work typically fails the 'duties test' for exemption

promptTemplate: You're offered an exempt salary of $80,000 OR a non-exempt role at $35/hr with regular 50-hour weeks. Which earns more annually?
explanationTemplate: Non-exempt calculation: (40 × $35 × 52) + (10 × $35 × 1.5 × 52) = $72,800 + $27,300 = $100,100/year. Exempt is fixed at $80,000. Non-exempt wins by $20k IF the overtime is consistent and tracked — but it loses flexibility and may carry stigma.
conceptChoices: Exempt salary ($80k) — guaranteed pay regardless of hours
Non-exempt — approximately $100,100/year with the 10 hours/week of overtime
They're equivalent — exempt has better benefits to make up the difference
Depends on the state's overtime laws
correctConceptChoice: Non-exempt — approximately $100,100/year with the 10 hours/week of overtime

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to your traditional 401(k) this month. Your marginal tax rate is {{marginalRate}}%. How much do you save in income tax?
explanationTemplate: Tax saved = contribution × marginal rate. ${{contribution}} × {{marginalRate}}% = ${{answer}}. This is what the IRS effectively 'pays' toward your contribution via the tax break.

promptTemplate: Your ${{contribution}}/month traditional 401(k) contribution at a {{marginalRate}}% marginal tax rate costs you how much in actual take-home pay?
explanationTemplate: Net cost = contribution × (1 − rate). ${{contribution}} × (1 − {{marginalRate}}%) = ${{answer}}. The other ${{contribution}} − ${{answer}} is the income tax you didn't pay.

promptTemplate: High earner in the {{marginalRate}}% federal + state bracket contributes ${{contribution}}/month to a traditional 401(k). What's the real take-home cost?
explanationTemplate: At higher brackets, the tax break is bigger. ${{contribution}} × (1 − {{marginalRate}}%) = ${{answer}} take-home cost. The high earner gets a much larger 'discount' on their retirement contribution than a low-bracket worker.

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}}/month to a traditional 401(k). At a {{marginalRate}}% bracket, how much tax do you save in a full year?
explanationTemplate: Annual tax saved: contribution × marginal rate (per month, then your math). The full-year version uses 12× monthly. This template tests the per-month version: ${{contribution}} × {{marginalRate}}% = ${{answer}}/month tax saving.

promptTemplate: Salary $80k, contributing 6% pre-tax ($400/month) at 22% bracket. Employer matches 50% up to 6%. What's your real take-home cost per month for the full contribution + match?
explanationTemplate: Your $400 contribution costs $400 × (1 − 22%) = $312 take-home. The employer match of $200 is FREE — they pay it; you pay nothing. Total into retirement: $600/mo. Real take-home cost: $312/mo. You're effectively buying $600 of retirement savings for $312 — a 92% instant 'return' before any market growth.
conceptChoices: $400 — the full contribution amount
$312 — contribution net of tax savings; the employer match is free money
$600 — contribution plus match
$200 — only the match
correctConceptChoice: $312 — contribution net of tax savings; the employer match is free money

promptTemplate: A 'share of stock' represents...
explanationTemplate: A share of stock is a small slice of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your share is worth more (and may pay dividends). If it does poorly, your share is worth less. Owners share in both upside and downside.
conceptChoices: A loan you made to the company
Partial ownership in a company
A bet on whether the company's price will rise
A guaranteed dividend payment
correctConceptChoice: Partial ownership in a company

promptTemplate: A bond represents...
explanationTemplate: When you buy a bond, you're lending money to the issuer (a government or corporation). They pay you interest for a set period, then return your principal. Lower risk than stocks, lower expected return.
conceptChoices: Partial ownership in a company
A loan you've made to a company or government, repaid with interest
A type of insurance policy
A bet on which way interest rates will move
correctConceptChoice: A loan you've made to a company or government, repaid with interest

promptTemplate: An index fund is...
explanationTemplate: An index fund holds every stock in a market index in proportion. The S&P 500 index fund owns shares in all 500 companies. No manager picks winners — you 'buy the market'. Decades of data show this beats most actively managed funds long-term.
conceptChoices: A fund managed by experts who pick winning stocks
A fund that owns all stocks in a market index (like the S&P 500), passively managed with low fees
A guaranteed-return savings account
A fund that only buys companies with low stock prices
correctConceptChoice: A fund that owns all stocks in a market index (like the S&P 500), passively managed with low fees

promptTemplate: The main practical difference between an ETF and a mutual fund is...
explanationTemplate: Both are baskets of investments. ETFs trade on exchanges (you can buy/sell at any price during market hours). Mutual funds settle once daily at the day's close. For long-term passive investing, the difference rarely matters. Both can be index funds.
conceptChoices: ETFs always have lower fees than mutual funds
ETFs trade like stocks throughout the day; mutual funds settle once per day at the closing price
ETFs are riskier than mutual funds
Mutual funds are tax-free; ETFs are not
correctConceptChoice: ETFs trade like stocks throughout the day; mutual funds settle once per day at the closing price

promptTemplate: Rank from highest historical risk AND return to lowest: index fund, individual stock, government bond, savings account.
explanationTemplate: Individual stocks have the widest range of outcomes (could double or go to zero). Index funds spread that risk across hundreds of companies — still volatile but less extreme. Government bonds are much steadier with lower returns. Savings accounts are essentially risk-free with the lowest returns.
conceptChoices: Savings account > Bond > Index fund > Individual stock
Individual stock > Index fund > Government bond > Savings account
Index fund > Individual stock > Savings account > Bond
All are equivalent over a long enough time horizon
correctConceptChoice: Individual stock > Index fund > Government bond > Savings account

promptTemplate: Using the '120 minus your age' rule of thumb, a 30-year-old should hold roughly what % in stocks?
explanationTemplate: 120 − 30 = 90% stocks. The rule lets younger investors take more risk for higher returns because they have decades to recover from any crash. As you age, the formula shifts you toward bonds for stability.
conceptChoices: 30% in stocks, 70% in bonds
50% in stocks, 50% in bonds
90% in stocks, 10% in bonds
100% in stocks, 0% in bonds
correctConceptChoice: 90% in stocks, 10% in bonds

promptTemplate: Why do most balanced portfolios include bonds alongside stocks?
explanationTemplate: Bonds typically rise (or fall less) when stocks fall, smoothing returns. The smoother ride matters because volatility tempts investors to sell at the worst moments. Even at lower expected returns, bonds keep you invested through downturns.
conceptChoices: Bonds always outperform stocks long-term
Bonds reduce volatility — they cushion the portfolio when stocks fall, lowering the risk of selling at a bad time
Bonds are required by law in all retirement accounts
Bonds eliminate all investment risk
correctConceptChoice: Bonds reduce volatility — they cushion the portfolio when stocks fall, lowering the risk of selling at a bad time

promptTemplate: A 'target-date 2050' fund automatically does what?
explanationTemplate: Target-date funds 'glide' from aggressive (stocks-heavy) when you're young to conservative (bonds-heavy) as the target year nears. They auto-rebalance — set it and forget it. The right default for most 401k participants.
conceptChoices: Pays out all your money in 2050
Shifts from stock-heavy to bond-heavy as 2050 approaches, reducing risk near retirement
Guarantees a minimum return by 2050
Only accepts contributions until 2050
correctConceptChoice: Shifts from stock-heavy to bond-heavy as 2050 approaches, reducing risk near retirement

promptTemplate: A 28-year-old has 60% bonds, 40% stocks in their 401k. What's the likely issue?
explanationTemplate: At 28, you have 30+ years of compounding ahead. Bonds historically return ~3-5%/year; stocks ~10%. Over 30 years that gap compounds into hundreds of thousands of dollars. The 60% bonds allocation gives up returns to avoid volatility they have decades to ride out.
conceptChoices: Perfect allocation for their age
Too conservative — they have 30+ years to compound and bonds will significantly underperform stocks over that horizon
Too aggressive — should be 100% bonds at this age
Doesn't matter — performance is identical over the long run
correctConceptChoice: Too conservative — they have 30+ years to compound and bonds will significantly underperform stocks over that horizon

promptTemplate: Your 100%-stocks portfolio drops 40% during a market crash. What's the historically best response?
explanationTemplate: The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in its history, including the Great Depression. Selling locks in losses; holding lets the recovery work for you. Continuing contributions during a crash means you're buying at discounted prices — exactly what DCA is for.
conceptChoices: Sell everything to protect against further losses
Move everything to bonds permanently — stocks are too risky
Do nothing — keep contributing on schedule. Markets have recovered from every prior crash within 1-7 years.
Try to time the bottom by buying heavily on the worst day
correctConceptChoice: Do nothing — keep contributing on schedule. Markets have recovered from every prior crash within 1-7 years.

promptTemplate: 'Loss aversion' is the finding that...
explanationTemplate: Kahneman and Tversky's research showed that losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. This asymmetry drives panic-selling — the pain of paper losses overwhelms rational thinking.
conceptChoices: Investors prefer losses over equivalent gains
Losses hurt about 2× more emotionally than equivalent gains feel good
Most investors avoid the stock market entirely
Losing money makes you smarter about investing
correctConceptChoice: Losses hurt about 2× more emotionally than equivalent gains feel good

promptTemplate: Your portfolio drops 25% in a week. You feel panic and start moving everything to cash. Which behavioral trap is this?
explanationTemplate: Loss aversion (often combined with recency bias) drives panic-selling. The pain of seeing a 25% drop feels much bigger than the gain of any future recovery, so people sell to 'stop the bleeding' — locking in losses just before recoveries.
conceptChoices: Loss aversion — emotional pain of the loss is overwhelming rational judgment
The Dunning-Kruger effect — overestimating your market knowledge
Survivor bias — only seeing successful investors
Anchoring — fixating on the original purchase price
correctConceptChoice: Loss aversion — emotional pain of the loss is overwhelming rational judgment

promptTemplate: True or false: 'A smart investor can time the market by carefully reading financial news.'
explanationTemplate: Decades of research (SPIVA reports, Morningstar studies) show that fewer than 20% of active fund managers beat their benchmarks over 10+ years. If trained professionals can't time markets, individual investors can't either. The solution: don't try — just keep buying.
conceptChoices: True — news always reflects future market direction
True — only if you read multiple sources
False — academic studies consistently show even professional fund managers fail to time markets reliably
True for individual stocks but false for index funds
correctConceptChoice: False — academic studies consistently show even professional fund managers fail to time markets reliably

promptTemplate: You have $20k to invest but want to 'wait for the next dip' before buying. The market has been up 25% over the year you've waited. What happened?
explanationTemplate: Markets spend more time going up than going down. Waiting for a dip usually means watching gains compound without you. By the time a real dip arrives, the market is often still above your original entry point. Lump-sum or DCA — but get in.
conceptChoices: You're now in a strong position — the dip is coming any day now
You missed gains while waiting. 'Wait for the dip' often means missing both the dip's start AND the subsequent recovery.
You preserved purchasing power — cash is king
You should keep waiting longer for the inevitable correction
correctConceptChoice: You missed gains while waiting. 'Wait for the dip' often means missing both the dip's start AND the subsequent recovery.

promptTemplate: Investors who panic-sold during the March 2020 COVID crash and stayed in cash for 12 months experienced what compared to those who held?
