explanationTemplate: From the March 2020 low to March 2021, the S&P 500 rose ~70%. Panic-sellers locked in 30%+ losses, then watched the recovery from the sidelines. The S&P hit new all-time highs by August 2020 — just five months after the crash. The behavioral discipline of doing nothing was worth more than any stock pick.
conceptChoices: Outperformed by avoiding the second wave of the pandemic
Broke even — bought back at similar prices to where they sold
Missed a ~70% recovery in the S&P 500 within 12 months — lost both the drop AND the rebound
Made identical returns because the crash was temporary
correctConceptChoice: Missed a ~70% recovery in the S&P 500 within 12 months — lost both the drop AND the rebound

promptTemplate: Which is the LARGEST single factor in your FICO credit score?
explanationTemplate: Payment history is 35% — the single biggest factor. One late payment can drop your score 50-100 points and stays on your report for 7 years. Utilization is second at 30%. Together those two factors are 65% of your score.
conceptChoices: Payment history (35%)
Credit utilization (30%)
Length of credit history (15%)
Number of credit inquiries (10%)
correctConceptChoice: Payment history (35%)

promptTemplate: What's the generally recommended MAXIMUM credit card utilization (balance ÷ limit) to protect your credit score?
explanationTemplate: 30% is the widely cited threshold — above this, your score starts to drop measurably. Ideal is under 10% if you want to maximize your score. Note: utilization is reported at statement close, not when you make a payment — so timing matters.
conceptChoices: Under 10%
Under 30%
Under 50%
Under 90% — as long as you pay it off each month
correctConceptChoice: Under 30%

promptTemplate: You decide to close your oldest credit card to 'simplify' your finances. What's the most likely impact on your score?
explanationTemplate: Closing an old card hurts two ways: it eventually drops off your report (shortening credit history) and immediately reduces your total available credit (raising your utilization ratio). If a card has no annual fee, keep it open even if unused.
conceptChoices: It will help — fewer cards is a positive signal
It will hurt — shortens your average credit age AND reduces your total credit limit (raising utilization)
No impact — closed cards don't count toward your score
Triggers a hard inquiry that hurts temporarily
correctConceptChoice: It will hurt — shortens your average credit age AND reduces your total credit limit (raising utilization)

promptTemplate: You apply for a new credit card, triggering a hard inquiry. What's the typical impact on your FICO score?
explanationTemplate: Hard inquiries typically cost 5-10 points and fade within 12-24 months. They stay on your report for 2 years but stop affecting your score after about 12 months. Multiple inquiries in a short period for the same type of loan (e.g., mortgage rate shopping) usually count as one.
conceptChoices: 50-100 point drop that persists for 7 years
5-10 point temporary drop that fades over 12-24 months
No impact — only utilization and payment history matter
It actually helps your score by adding new available credit
correctConceptChoice: 5-10 point temporary drop that fades over 12-24 months

promptTemplate: True or false: 'You need to carry a credit card balance month-to-month to build credit.'
explanationTemplate: The myth that you must carry debt to build credit is one of the most expensive misconceptions in personal finance. FICO rewards using credit and paying it back — the interest charges are just the cost of NOT paying in full. Use cards regularly and pay the full statement balance every month.
conceptChoices: True — utilization above 0% is required
True — only interest charges count toward payment history
False — paying in full every month builds credit perfectly well. You need credit ACTIVITY, not interest payments.
True for the first 6 months only
correctConceptChoice: False — paying in full every month builds credit perfectly well. You need credit ACTIVITY, not interest payments.

promptTemplate: Which debt scores best across the four factors (rate, asset, cash flow, tax treatment)?
explanationTemplate: The 6% mortgage on a 10+ year hold scores well on all four factors: rate (below long-term stock returns), asset (home appreciates), cash flow (typically manageable as part of 28%-rule rent budget), and tax treatment (mortgage interest is deductible up to AGI limits).
conceptChoices: Buy-now-pay-later for clothes
Credit card balance at 22% APR
A 6% mortgage on a home you plan to live in for 10+ years
A 12% personal loan for a vacation
correctConceptChoice: A 6% mortgage on a home you plan to live in for 10+ years

promptTemplate: Which is typically considered 'bad debt'?
explanationTemplate: 24% APR is far above any reasonable investment return and far above tax-deductible thresholds. Carrying a credit card balance month-to-month is the textbook definition of bad debt — high rate, no asset built, no tax benefit.
conceptChoices: A mortgage at 5%
A federal student loan at 5%
A credit card balance at 24% APR carried month-to-month
A car loan at 4% on a needed vehicle
correctConceptChoice: A credit card balance at 24% APR carried month-to-month

promptTemplate: Using the 4-factor framework (rate, asset, cash flow, tax), what's the rate band where debt becomes almost-always bad regardless of the other factors?
explanationTemplate: Above ~10%, the rate factor dominates the other three. Long-term stock returns average ~10% nominal (per S&P historical); debt above that is mathematically destructive — even if the asset is great and the loan is tax-deductible, the rate kills the math. Under 6%: usually fine. 6-10%: depends on the other factors. 10%+: almost always bad.
conceptChoices: Above 2%
Above 8-10% (where interest cost typically exceeds long-term investment returns)
Above 15%
Above 20%
correctConceptChoice: Above 8-10% (where interest cost typically exceeds long-term investment returns)

promptTemplate: You take a $600,000 mortgage on a home. 18 months later, your job moves you to another city. Is this still 'good debt'?
explanationTemplate: The 'good debt' framing of a mortgage assumes you hold long enough to (1) recover closing costs (~3-5% of purchase price) and (2) build meaningful equity. 18 months rarely covers either. With selling costs of 6-8%, a short ownership often costs more than renting would have.
conceptChoices: Yes — mortgages are always good debt no matter the timeline
Less so — short ownership timeline means closing costs + selling fees + potential price drop probably exceed any equity gained
Yes, as long as you can rent the property out
It depends on the federal interest rate at the time
correctConceptChoice: Less so — short ownership timeline means closing costs + selling fees + potential price drop probably exceed any equity gained

promptTemplate: You have $5,000 extra cash. Option A: pay off a $5,000 credit card balance at 22% APR. Option B: invest in an index fund averaging 8%. Which is mathematically correct?
explanationTemplate: Paying off 22% debt is mathematically a guaranteed 22% return. Investing at 8% is expected return — uncertain, possibly lower. The 14-point gap makes payoff the obvious choice. The general rule: pay off debt above 8% before investing beyond the 401k match.
conceptChoices: Invest — index funds always beat debt payoff over time
Pay off the credit card — 22% guaranteed return beats 8% expected return
Split it 50/50 to diversify
Save it as cash for an emergency
correctConceptChoice: Pay off the credit card — 22% guaranteed return beats 8% expected return

promptTemplate: You have $0 saved, $4,000 in credit card debt at 24% APR, and an unexpected $500 to allocate. In the standard 'Order of Operations,' what should you do first?
explanationTemplate: Build a $1,000 starter emergency fund first (per r/personalfinance's Order of Operations and Dave Ramsey's Baby Step 1). Without it, the next small emergency (car repair, medical co-pay) goes right onto the same credit card, growing the principal and erasing any payoff progress. The starter EF protects your debt-payoff plan from getting reset by life. THEN attack the 24% debt aggressively.
conceptChoices: Throw all $500 at the credit card — interest savings beat any cash hoarding
Build a $1,000 starter emergency fund first, then attack the 24% debt — the EF stops a small emergency from running up more debt
Invest in index funds — long-run returns beat 24% APR
Split exactly 50/50 between EF and debt
correctConceptChoice: Build a $1,000 starter emergency fund first, then attack the 24% debt — the EF stops a small emergency from running up more debt

promptTemplate: You have $1k emergency fund, $3k in credit card debt at 20% APR, and your employer offers a 100% 401(k) match up to 5% of your salary. What's the priority order for your next dollars?
explanationTemplate: 401(k) match comes before high-interest debt in the Order of Operations because a 100% match is an instant doubling — no investment return can beat that. Capture the match first; everything beyond the match goes to the 20% APR debt next. You're not 'investing instead of paying off debt' — you're collecting the free money your employer is offering, then immediately attacking the debt with everything else.
conceptChoices: Credit card payoff first, then 401(k) match — debt always before investing
401(k) match first (instant 100% return), THEN the 20% credit card — match is free money you only get by contributing
Skip the match until you're debt-free
Half to each
correctConceptChoice: 401(k) match first (instant 100% return), THEN the 20% credit card — match is free money you only get by contributing

promptTemplate: You have $1k EF, no employer 401(k) match, and $2,500 in credit card debt at 22% APR. Should you build your EF to 3-6 months of essentials before paying off the card?
explanationTemplate: No — pay off the high-interest debt first. 22% APR is a guaranteed loss bigger than any plausible investment return. The $1k starter EF you already have is enough to bridge most small emergencies; building a full EF while paying 22% interest on the card means losing ~$45/month every month you delay. Per the Order of Operations: $1k starter → debt above ~8% → THEN full EF.
conceptChoices: Yes — emergency fund is always priority #1
No — pay off the 22% debt first. A guaranteed 22% 'return' beats any reason to expand the EF beyond the $1k starter.
Yes — but only build to 1 month, not 3-6
No — invest in stocks instead of doing either
correctConceptChoice: No — pay off the 22% debt first. A guaranteed 22% 'return' beats any reason to expand the EF beyond the $1k starter.

promptTemplate: You have a $5k emergency fund and your only debt is a 3.5% mortgage. You have $500/month extra cash flow. What does the Order of Operations suggest?
explanationTemplate: Below the ~8% threshold (long-run stock market returns), the math favors investing over extra debt payoff. A 3.5% mortgage is well below that — invest the $500 in retirement accounts (capture any remaining match, then max IRA/401(k)/HSA). The 'pay off the mortgage' impulse is psychological, not mathematical. Same money invested at 7-10% beats accelerated mortgage payoff in expected value.
conceptChoices: Throw it all at the mortgage — debt-free is always best
Invest it — at 3.5% mortgage vs ~10% expected stock returns, the math favors investing. Mortgage payoff is psychological, not mathematical, below 8%.
Build the EF larger first
Save it as cash
correctConceptChoice: Invest it — at 3.5% mortgage vs ~10% expected stock returns, the math favors investing. Mortgage payoff is psychological, not mathematical, below 8%.

promptTemplate: Mid-career professional: $0 EF, $8k credit card debt at 24% APR, $200k mortgage at 6.5%, employer matches 50% up to 6% (currently contributing 0%). $2,000/month free cash flow. What's the standard Order of Operations sequence?
explanationTemplate: (1) Build $1k starter EF (one month of $2k cash flow). (2) Start 6% 401(k) contribution to capture the full 50% match (instant 50% return on those dollars). (3) Attack the 24% APR credit card with the remaining cash flow until paid off (this is the biggest guaranteed return left). (4) Build full 3-6 month EF of essentials. (5) Address the 6.5% mortgage only after maxing retirement accounts — at 6.5% it's borderline but still below long-run stock returns, so investing usually wins. The mortgage is the LAST priority despite feeling psychologically urgent.
conceptChoices: (1) Pay off credit card (2) full EF (3) match (4) mortgage extra (5) invest
(1) $1k starter EF (2) 401(k) match (3) credit card payoff (4) full EF (5) max retirement, mortgage extra is last
(1) Mortgage payoff (2) credit card (3) EF (4) match (5) investing
(1) Max 401(k) (2) credit card (3) EF (4) mortgage (5) starter EF
correctConceptChoice: (1) $1k starter EF (2) 401(k) match (3) credit card payoff (4) full EF (5) max retirement, mortgage extra is last

promptTemplate: You're planning to live in a city for less than 3 years. What does the standard buy-vs-rent rule say?
explanationTemplate: The 5-year rule: stay under 5 years, you rarely break even on a purchase. Closing costs alone (2-5% buying + 6% selling = ~10% round-trip) typically exceed any appreciation or principal paydown in such a short timeline.
conceptChoices: Buy — building equity is always better than renting
Rent — closing costs (2-5%) and selling fees (~6%) usually eat any equity gains in under 5 years
Buy only if you can put 20% down
Buy a smaller property to keep costs low
correctConceptChoice: Rent — closing costs (2-5%) and selling fees (~6%) usually eat any equity gains in under 5 years

promptTemplate: You're committed to a city for 10+ years and rents are rising 5%/year. The buy-vs-rent math typically favors...
explanationTemplate: 10+ year horizons favor buying because: (1) closing costs amortize over many years, (2) you build equity through principal paydown and (usually) appreciation, (3) your mortgage payment stays fixed while rent rises 3-5%/year. Even modest appreciation compounds significantly.
conceptChoices: Renting — flexibility is always more valuable than equity
Buying — long timeline lets amortization and appreciation compound, and fixed mortgage payments beat rising rents
Renting — homes always lose value long-term
Either equally — it's a wash over 10 years
correctConceptChoice: Buying — long timeline lets amortization and appreciation compound, and fixed mortgage payments beat rising rents

promptTemplate: Why does the old 'rent × 200 = break-even purchase price' rule break down in a 7% mortgage-rate environment?
explanationTemplate: The rent × 200 rule comes from an era of 3-4% mortgage rates. At 7%, the same purchase price has a much higher monthly mortgage payment, shifting the break-even multiplier down to roughly 150-180. At today's rates, you'd want rent × ~165 < purchase price for buying to compete — not the old × 200.
conceptChoices: The rule still works — interest rates don't affect the rent-vs-buy break-even
Higher mortgage rates make the same purchase price more expensive monthly, so the break-even multiplier drops to ~150-180
Property taxes have eaten the rule
Rent has stopped growing
correctConceptChoice: Higher mortgage rates make the same purchase price more expensive monthly, so the break-even multiplier drops to ~150-180

promptTemplate: You're choosing between renting (and investing $60k in an index fund) vs putting $60k down on a home. What's the 'opportunity cost' factor most people forget?
explanationTemplate: The down payment isn't 'free' — it has an opportunity cost. $60k invested at the long-term S&P 500 average (~8%) becomes ~$129k after 10 years. If your home equity grows less than that over the same period (very possible in flat markets), renting + investing wins.
conceptChoices: Investment returns are unpredictable, so they don't count
$60k invested at 8% becomes ~$129k after 10 years; your $60k home equity may not grow as much
Opportunity cost only applies to business investments
It only matters if you can guarantee 10%+ returns
correctConceptChoice: $60k invested at 8% becomes ~$129k after 10 years; your $60k home equity may not grow as much

promptTemplate: Your career involves regular relocations (every 2-4 years). What does this mean for buy vs rent?
explanationTemplate: Careers with regular relocations (military, consulting, tech, medical residency) almost always favor renting. Each move triggers 6-10% in transaction costs. Renting out as a long-distance landlord adds management headaches and is rarely profitable on a primary residence.
conceptChoices: Buy — you can rent out each home as you leave, building a rental empire
Rent strongly — mobility-required careers almost always make buying a financial loser due to transaction costs
Buy only if you can flip homes for profit
Doesn't matter — the math is the same
correctConceptChoice: Rent strongly — mobility-required careers almost always make buying a financial loser due to transaction costs

promptTemplate: What's a 'reasonable' early termination fee in most US rental markets?
explanationTemplate: Industry standard for reasonable early termination: 1-2 months of rent. Anything 3+ months is aggressive; 4+ is predatory in most markets. Some states require landlords to make 'reasonable efforts to re-rent' (mitigation duty) regardless of the contract amount.
conceptChoices: Half of one month's rent
1-2 months of rent
6 months of rent
A full year of rent
correctConceptChoice: 1-2 months of rent

promptTemplate: Your lease has an automatic renewal clause requiring 90 days' notice to terminate. What's the trap?
explanationTemplate: Auto-renewal traps are designed to lock in tenants through inattention. With a 90-day notice for a 12-month lease, you must remember to act 3 months before lease end. Calendar reminders are essential. Some states have started restricting these clauses but most still allow them.
conceptChoices: There's no trap — 90 days is generous
You may forget the notice window and find yourself locked into another full lease year
Auto-renewal is illegal in all US states
The notice period only applies to month-to-month leases
correctConceptChoice: You may forget the notice window and find yourself locked into another full lease year

promptTemplate: Your landlord must return your security deposit within...
explanationTemplate: Security deposit return timelines are state-regulated. Most states require 14-60 days, with itemized deductions if any. If a landlord violates this, you may be entitled to 2-3× the deposit back as penalty. Always document the unit's condition at move-in and move-out with photos.
conceptChoices: 30 days after you move out (varies by state, typically 14-60 days)
1 year after lease end
Only when they find a new tenant
Whenever they choose — there's no legal deadline
correctConceptChoice: 30 days after you move out (varies by state, typically 14-60 days)

promptTemplate: Which lease clause is likely UNENFORCEABLE in most US states (even if you sign it)?
explanationTemplate: Most states require landlords to maintain habitability (working heat, plumbing, structural integrity) — clauses shifting these duties to tenants are typically unenforceable regardless of what the lease says. Other common unenforceable clauses: waivers of right to sue, blanket non-refundable deposits.
conceptChoices: Pets prohibited
'Tenant responsible for all property repairs including landlord's responsibilities under state law'
Rent due on the 1st of the month
Security deposit of one month's rent
correctConceptChoice: 'Tenant responsible for all property repairs including landlord's responsibilities under state law'

promptTemplate: Your landlord deducts $200 from your deposit for 'cleaning' after a normal-use tenancy. Is this legitimate?
explanationTemplate: 'Normal wear and tear' (scuffs on walls, light cleaning needs, minor carpet wear) is the cost of doing business. Deductions are legal for actual damage beyond normal use (large holes, broken fixtures, heavy stains). Many tenants successfully challenge improper deductions in small claims court.
conceptChoices: Yes — landlords can always deduct cleaning fees
Usually no — 'normal wear and tear' (including standard cleaning) is the landlord's cost, not deductible from the deposit
Yes if it's in the lease
Only if the unit was professionally cleaned at move-in
correctConceptChoice: Usually no — 'normal wear and tear' (including standard cleaning) is the landlord's cost, not deductible from the deposit

promptTemplate: What does FICA on your paycheck cover?
explanationTemplate: FICA = Federal Insurance Contributions Act. It funds Social Security (6.2% on wages up to $184,500 in 2026) and Medicare (1.45% on all wages, with 0.9% extra on wages over $200k). Employers match this dollar-for-dollar, so the true tax is 15.3% — self-employed people pay both halves.
conceptChoices: Federal income tax
Social Security + Medicare (7.65% combined: 6.2% SS + 1.45% Medicare)
State income tax
Health insurance
correctConceptChoice: Social Security + Medicare (7.65% combined: 6.2% SS + 1.45% Medicare)

promptTemplate: Which of these reduces BOTH your federal income tax AND your FICA (Social Security + Medicare) tax?
explanationTemplate: HSA contributions made via payroll deduction (Section 125 cafeteria plan) reduce both federal income tax AND FICA. Traditional 401k contributions reduce federal income tax only — they're still subject to FICA. This is one of the HSA's underrated advantages.
conceptChoices: Traditional 401k contribution
HSA contribution via payroll deduction
Roth IRA contribution
Wage garnishment for credit card debt
correctConceptChoice: HSA contribution via payroll deduction

promptTemplate: For most married couples, the default and usually-best filing status is...
explanationTemplate: MFJ combines both incomes onto one return with wider brackets and a larger standard deduction. For most couples, this produces the lowest tax. MFS makes sense only in specific cases (IBR student loans, large itemized deductions for one spouse, separation).
conceptChoices: Single (filed separately for each spouse)
Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) — usually lower total tax
Married Filing Separately (MFS) — always saves money
Head of Household if at least one spouse works
correctConceptChoice: Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) — usually lower total tax

promptTemplate: A married couple where one spouse has heavy income-driven repayment (IDR) student loans should consider Married Filing Separately because...
explanationTemplate: On IDR plans (IBR, PAYE, SAVE), filing jointly means BOTH spouses' incomes count toward the payment calculation, often dramatically raising the IDR payment. MFS keeps each spouse's income separate. The trade-off: you may lose some tax credits and pay slightly more federal tax — but save much more on student loan payments.
conceptChoices: MFS always saves money for couples
IDR loan payments are calculated only on the borrower's income — MFS keeps the spouse's income out of the calculation
Student loans are tax-deductible only in MFS
It avoids garnishment of the spouse's wages
correctConceptChoice: IDR loan payments are calculated only on the borrower's income — MFS keeps the spouse's income out of the calculation

promptTemplate: A single parent providing > 50% of their child's household costs typically files as...
explanationTemplate: Single parents almost always qualify for Head of Household (HoH) — bigger standard deduction ($24,150 vs $16,100 in 2026), wider brackets, more generous credits. Many single parents file Single by mistake and overpay. The HoH qualification: unmarried + pay > 50% of household costs + qualifying dependent (usually a child).
conceptChoices: Single (the default for unmarried filers)
Head of Household (significantly larger standard deduction)
Married Filing Separately
Qualifying Widow(er) regardless of partner's status
correctConceptChoice: Head of Household (significantly larger standard deduction)

promptTemplate: Which insurance policy should typically be your HIGHEST priority?
explanationTemplate: Health insurance is the universal priority because medical bills can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars — they're the #1 cause of bankruptcy in the US. Even a healthy person's potential exposure (one accident, one diagnosis) is catastrophic without insurance.
conceptChoices: Pet insurance
Health insurance
Extended warranty on electronics
Identity theft insurance
correctConceptChoice: Health insurance

promptTemplate: Which insurance is most commonly oversold and overpaid for?
explanationTemplate: Extended warranties on electronics (phones, TVs, laptops) are almost always net negative. Consumer Reports data: most consumers don't use them, and average payouts are far below cost. Self-insure with an emergency fund instead — the manufacturer warranty covers the first year of defects.
conceptChoices: Health insurance
Disability insurance
Extended warranties on consumer electronics
Liability auto insurance
correctConceptChoice: Extended warranties on consumer electronics

promptTemplate: A 28-year-old with no dependents, no mortgage, and $20k in savings is most likely OVER-insured on...
explanationTemplate: Life insurance protects dependents from losing your income. With no dependents and no mortgage, the case for $1M coverage is weak — your debts/funeral costs might justify $50k-$100k, not $1M. Save the premium and put it toward retirement. The math changes the moment you have kids or buy a home.
conceptChoices: Health insurance
Renter's insurance
A $1 million life insurance policy
Disability insurance
correctConceptChoice: A $1 million life insurance policy

promptTemplate: For a 32-year-old working professional with no dependents, which is statistically MORE important — life insurance or disability insurance?
explanationTemplate: SSA data: ~25% of today's 20-year-olds will experience a disability lasting 90+ days before retirement. Death rate before 65 is ~5%. For working-age adults without dependents, disability insurance is statistically more important than life insurance — yet far fewer people carry adequate coverage.
conceptChoices: Life insurance — without it, your family has no protection
Disability insurance — you're roughly 5× more likely to be disabled for 90+ days than to die before retirement
Both equally important regardless of dependents
Neither matters at age 32
correctConceptChoice: Disability insurance — you're roughly 5× more likely to be disabled for 90+ days than to die before retirement

promptTemplate: You're offered a $300 extended warranty on a $1,200 laptop, covering years 2-3. The principle 'self-insure small risks, transfer catastrophic ones' suggests...
explanationTemplate: A $1,200 laptop is not catastrophic — you can self-insure. Save the $300 premium. Even if the laptop breaks in year 3 and needs full replacement ($1,200), your net cost is $1,200 − $300 saved = $900. But most laptops survive 3+ years, meaning you typically keep the full $300.
conceptChoices: Buy the warranty — laptops break unpredictably
Decline — $300 lost to warranty cost is small compared to the $900 you'd net by self-insuring (laptop replacement minus warranty premium)
Buy it only if you've had laptops break before
Always buy warranties — they pay for themselves
correctConceptChoice: Decline — $300 lost to warranty cost is small compared to the $900 you'd net by self-insuring (laptop replacement minus warranty premium)

promptTemplate: Statistically, how likely is a 20-year-old today to experience a disability lasting 90+ days before retirement?
explanationTemplate: Per Social Security Administration data, ~25% of today's 20-year-olds will experience a disability lasting 90+ days before reaching retirement age. This far exceeds the rate of early death (~5%), making disability insurance arguably more important than life insurance for working-age adults.
conceptChoices: About 5% — disability is rare
About 25% (1 in 4) — far more common than people realize
About 50% — virtually inevitable
About 1% — almost no one
correctConceptChoice: About 25% (1 in 4) — far more common than people realize

promptTemplate: An 'own-occupation' disability policy pays out if you can't perform...
explanationTemplate: 'Own-occupation' is the gold standard: it pays if you can't do YOUR job. A surgeon with a hand injury still qualifies even if they could teach. 'Any-occupation' is much weaker — pays only if you can't do ANY job (including minimum wage). Always check this distinction on employer LTD policies.
conceptChoices: ANY job at all (most restrictive)
YOUR SPECIFIC job — even if you could do a different job (much better for high earners)
Only physical labor jobs
Only your primary job, not side gigs
correctConceptChoice: YOUR SPECIFIC job — even if you could do a different job (much better for high earners)

promptTemplate: Employer-provided long-term disability typically caps monthly payouts at...
explanationTemplate: Most employer LTD plans pay 60% of base salary, capped at $5,000-$10,000/month ($60k-$120k/year). For someone earning $300k, this leaves a huge gap. High earners often need supplemental individual disability coverage to fill the gap.
conceptChoices: $5,000-$10,000/month, which under-insures high earners
Your full salary with no cap
Minimum wage equivalent
Only $1,000/month
correctConceptChoice: $5,000-$10,000/month, which under-insures high earners

promptTemplate: Your disability policy has a 90-day 'elimination period.' What does this mean for your emergency fund?
explanationTemplate: An elimination period is the waiting period before benefits begin (typically 90 days for long-term disability). During those 90 days, you have no income. This is why a 3-6 month emergency fund is essential even with disability insurance — to bridge the gap.
conceptChoices: You don't need an emergency fund — disability covers everything
You need at least 3 months of essential expenses saved to bridge the gap before benefits start
The elimination period only applies to short-term disability
You can get benefits starting day 1 if you negotiate
correctConceptChoice: You need at least 3 months of essential expenses saved to bridge the gap before benefits start

promptTemplate: A $250,000/year earner has employer-provided LTD at 60% of salary, capped at $10,000/month. What's their coverage gap?
explanationTemplate: True income replacement at 60% of $250k = $12,500/month. Employer LTD caps at $10k/month. Gap = $2,500/month = $30k/year of unreplaced income during disability. Supplemental individual disability policies can fill this gap — important for high earners.
conceptChoices: No gap — 60% covers everything
$2,500/month — employer covers $10k/mo (the cap), but 60% of $250k would be ~$12,500/mo (uncapped)
$5,000/month gap because of taxes
There's no way to know without more info
correctConceptChoice: $2,500/month — employer covers $10k/mo (the cap), but 60% of $250k would be ~$12,500/mo (uncapped)

promptTemplate: When buying a car, what's the SINGLE number you should negotiate?
explanationTemplate: Always negotiate OTD price. Dealers love to switch the conversation to monthly payment (they'll extend the loan term to lower it) or trade-in (they'll lowball that and inflate the car price). OTD locks in your total cost — everything else is theater.
conceptChoices: Monthly payment — what you can afford
Out-the-door (OTD) price — total cost including all fees, taxes, and add-ons
Trade-in value of your old car
Down payment amount
correctConceptChoice: Out-the-door (OTD) price — total cost including all fees, taxes, and add-ons

promptTemplate: A dealer says 'I can get you down to $400/month.' Why is focusing on monthly payment a trap?
explanationTemplate: The 'monthly payment trap' lets dealers control your total cost without you noticing. $500/mo × 60 months = $30k. $400/mo × 84 months = $33,600 — same car, $3,600 more paid. Always think in total cost, not monthly comfort.
conceptChoices: Monthly payments are illegal in some states
Dealers can lower monthly by extending the loan term — same car, more interest, more total paid
Monthly payments include hidden insurance
It's not a trap — monthly payment is what matters
correctConceptChoice: Dealers can lower monthly by extending the loan term — same car, more interest, more total paid

promptTemplate: The F&I (Finance & Insurance) office is where dealers pitch...
explanationTemplate: F&I is where dealers make significant profit. The pitched add-ons (extended warranties at 100-300% markup, GAP insurance at 3-5× independent prices, paint protection that's basically wax) are almost always available cheaper elsewhere. Decline everything in F&I and shop separately if interested.
conceptChoices: Negotiable car price
Add-ons like extended warranties, GAP insurance, paint protection — almost always at marked-up prices
Free vehicle maintenance plans
Cash discounts for paying upfront
correctConceptChoice: Add-ons like extended warranties, GAP insurance, paint protection — almost always at marked-up prices

promptTemplate: Your bank pre-approves you at 5.5% APR. The dealer 'magically' offers you 7% APR. What's happening?
explanationTemplate: Dealers earn commission by marking up financing rates 1-3% above what the lender quoted them. On a $30k loan over 5 years, a 1.5% markup costs you ~$1,200 extra in interest. Always get pre-approved from your bank or credit union BEFORE walking into the dealership. Then make them beat your rate or you'll bring your own.
conceptChoices: The dealer has access to better rates than your bank
The lender quoted the dealer 5.5% and the dealer marked it up 1.5% — the markup is dealer profit on your financing
Dealer financing always has higher interest
The dealer is being honest about market rates
correctConceptChoice: The lender quoted the dealer 5.5% and the dealer marked it up 1.5% — the markup is dealer profit on your financing

promptTemplate: GAP insurance from the dealer costs $800. Your credit union offers the same coverage for $200. What's the smart play?
explanationTemplate: GAP insurance from credit unions or independent providers typically costs $200-$400 for the same coverage dealers sell for $600-$1,200. Same product, 60-75% markup at the dealer. Decline at signing — you can always add it later from a cheaper source.
conceptChoices: Take the dealer's GAP — it's bundled into your loan, easier
Decline at the dealer and buy from the credit union — saves $600 for identical coverage
Skip GAP entirely — it's never worth it
Negotiate the dealer down to $400
correctConceptChoice: Decline at the dealer and buy from the credit union — saves $600 for identical coverage

promptTemplate: A typical new car's MANUFACTURER warranty covers...
explanationTemplate: Industry standard new-car coverage: 3yr/36k bumper-to-bumper (covers almost everything), 5yr/60k powertrain (engine, transmission, drivetrain). Some brands (Kia, Hyundai) offer longer powertrain warranties (10yr/100k). Extended warranties from dealers add coverage AFTER the manufacturer warranty expires.
conceptChoices: Lifetime of the car at no extra charge
Usually 3 years / 36,000 miles bumper-to-bumper, plus 5 years / 60,000 miles powertrain
Only the engine and nothing else
Only the first 10,000 miles
correctConceptChoice: Usually 3 years / 36,000 miles bumper-to-bumper, plus 5 years / 60,000 miles powertrain

promptTemplate: An extended warranty costs $2,000 for 5 years. You estimate a 30% chance of needing a covered repair averaging $2,500 in that window. What's the expected-value math?
explanationTemplate: Expected value = probability × payout − cost. Here: 30% × $2,500 = $750 expected payout, vs $2,000 cost = −$1,250 expected loss per warranty bought. Per Consumer Reports' multi-year owner surveys, this asymmetry is typical: most buyers never use the coverage, and those who do recoup less than they paid. Like most insurance, it's a transfer to the seller in exchange for peace of mind.
conceptChoices: EV = +$500 (warranty is a good deal)
EV = $0 (it's a fair bet)
EV = −$1,250 (warranty costs more than expected repairs)
Can't calculate without more info
correctConceptChoice: EV = −$1,250 (warranty costs more than expected repairs)

promptTemplate: Instead of a $2,000 extended warranty, you could save $33/month for 5 years. What's the financial advantage?
explanationTemplate: Self-insurance = save the premium you would've paid into a 'repair fund.' For most reliable brands (Toyota, Honda, Lexus, Mazda), the savings exceed average repair costs over 5 years. For luxury European or first-gen EVs, extended warranties have stronger cases.
conceptChoices: None — extended warranties are always better than self-insuring
If no major repair occurs (likely), you keep the full $2,000. Even with one major repair, you may come out ahead or break even.
Self-insuring is illegal in most states
Banks don't allow you to self-insure cars
correctConceptChoice: If no major repair occurs (likely), you keep the full $2,000. Even with one major repair, you may come out ahead or break even.

promptTemplate: An extended warranty is MOST likely to be worth the cost for which type of vehicle?
explanationTemplate: Extended warranties make sense in narrow cases: (1) first-year vehicles with unknown reliability, (2) high-repair-cost vehicles like luxury European brands, (3) EVs with expensive battery replacement risk. Pass on extended warranties for Toyota/Honda/Mazda — these brands rarely need post-warranty major repairs.
conceptChoices: A used Toyota Camry with 50k miles
A first-year electric vehicle from a new manufacturer (limited repair data, expensive battery)
Any used minivan
Vehicles you plan to sell within 2 years
correctConceptChoice: A first-year electric vehicle from a new manufacturer (limited repair data, expensive battery)

promptTemplate: 'Certified Pre-Owned' (CPO) from a manufacturer typically includes...
explanationTemplate: CPO is the rare case where extended coverage is built in. The manufacturer (not a third party) extends warranty coverage AND performs an inspection. CPO cars cost more than identical non-CPO used cars but the warranty value often justifies the premium — especially for higher-end vehicles with expensive repair risks.
conceptChoices: Nothing extra — it's just a marketing label
An extended manufacturer-backed warranty AND a multi-point inspection — adds real value vs a regular used car
A guaranteed buyback option
Free oil changes for life
correctConceptChoice: An extended manufacturer-backed warranty AND a multi-point inspection — adds real value vs a regular used car

promptTemplate: A federal SUBSIDIZED student loan means...
explanationTemplate: Subsidized loans are an enormous benefit: the government pays your interest during in-school enrollment, the 6-month grace period, and approved deferment periods. Your loan balance stays at your borrowed amount until repayment begins.
conceptChoices: The government pays the interest while you're in school, during grace, and during deferment
You don't have to repay it at all
The interest is permanently waived
The loan has a lower interest rate than unsubsidized
correctConceptChoice: The government pays the interest while you're in school, during grace, and during deferment

promptTemplate: A federal UNSUBSIDIZED student loan means...
explanationTemplate: Unsubsidized loans accrue interest from the moment they're disbursed. By graduation, your $25k loan may have grown to $28k+ in interest. This unpaid interest then capitalizes (added to principal), so you pay interest on interest going forward. Most graduate loans and Parent PLUS are unsubsidized.
conceptChoices: The government waives interest if you stay enrolled
Interest accrues from day one — you owe interest while in school, during grace, and during deferment
You only pay interest if you earn over a certain income
The interest rate is variable
correctConceptChoice: Interest accrues from day one — you owe interest while in school, during grace, and during deferment

promptTemplate: Who qualifies for subsidized federal student loans?
explanationTemplate: Subsidized loans are restricted to undergraduate students with financial need (per FAFSA analysis). Graduate students and Parent PLUS borrowers don't get subsidized loans — their loans are all unsubsidized. If you qualify for any subsidized amount, take it first.
conceptChoices: Anyone who applies for federal aid
Only undergraduates with demonstrated financial need
Graduate students only
Parents borrowing on behalf of students
correctConceptChoice: Only undergraduates with demonstrated financial need

promptTemplate: You borrow $25,000 in UNSUBSIDIZED loans at 5.5% over 4 years of college plus a 6-month grace period. Approximately what's your balance at repayment start?
explanationTemplate: $25k × 5.5% × 4.5 years simple interest = $6,188 in accrued interest. At grace period end, this capitalizes (gets added to principal). Your new balance: ~$31,188. You then owe interest on the full $31k going forward — interest on interest. This is why grace period interest matters.
conceptChoices: $25,000 (no change)
About $31,000 (interest accrued during 4.5 years and capitalized)
About $20,000 (interest forgiven during grace)
About $50,000 (compound interest doubles)
correctConceptChoice: About $31,000 (interest accrued during 4.5 years and capitalized)

promptTemplate: True or false: 'Graduate students can borrow subsidized federal loans for graduate school.'
explanationTemplate: Since 2012, graduate students have lost access to subsidized loans. All graduate Direct Loans are unsubsidized, accruing interest from day one. This is one reason graduate school debt grows so fast — a $40k/year program can leave you owing $200k+ at repayment if you don't pay interest during enrollment.
conceptChoices: True — graduate students get the same options as undergrads
False — graduate Direct Loans are all UNSUBSIDIZED (interest accrues from day one)
True — but only for STEM fields
True — but the interest rate is higher
correctConceptChoice: False — graduate Direct Loans are all UNSUBSIDIZED (interest accrues from day one)

promptTemplate: When you refinance federal student loans to a private lender, what do you LOSE?
explanationTemplate: Refinancing federal loans to private is one-way and permanent. You forfeit ALL federal protections: income-driven repayment plans, Public Service Loan Forgiveness (10-year forgiveness for public service), federal forbearance during hardship, death/disability discharge, and any future federal relief programs (like COVID-era pauses). Many refi salespeople omit this.
conceptChoices: Only the federal interest rate
Federal protections: IDR, PSLF, federal forbearance, death/disability discharge, future federal relief — permanently
Nothing — refinancing only changes the rate
The ability to make payments online
correctConceptChoice: Federal protections: IDR, PSLF, federal forbearance, death/disability discharge, future federal relief — permanently

promptTemplate: If you refinance federal loans to private, can you refinance BACK to federal later?
explanationTemplate: This is the single most important fact about refinancing — it's irreversible. Once you go private, you cannot return to federal loans. Make this decision carefully. If you might ever need IDR, work in public service, face job loss, or want to keep optionality, do NOT refinance.
conceptChoices: Yes — you can switch any time
Yes, but only within 1 year
No — the move is permanent. You cannot refinance from private back to federal.
Yes, but you lose your interest rate
correctConceptChoice: No — the move is permanent. You cannot refinance from private back to federal.

promptTemplate: A public school teacher with federal student loans is offered a 2% rate reduction by refinancing to private. Should they refinance?
explanationTemplate: Public school teachers qualify for PSLF — 10 years of qualifying payments while working in public service leads to forgiveness of the entire remaining balance. On a $50k loan, PSLF can be worth $30k-$60k in forgiveness. Saving 2% on the rate doesn't come close. Never refinance if you're in public service.
conceptChoices: Yes — 2% rate savings is significant over 10 years
No — public school teachers qualify for PSLF, which forgives the remaining balance after 10 years. Refi forfeits this benefit.
Yes, but only if they plan to leave teaching
Yes — PSLF is being phased out anyway
correctConceptChoice: No — public school teachers qualify for PSLF, which forgives the remaining balance after 10 years. Refi forfeits this benefit.

promptTemplate: Refinancing federal loans to private makes sense ONLY when which is true?
explanationTemplate: Refi makes sense in narrow conditions: stable high earner (so IDR is irrelevant), no public service work (so PSLF doesn't apply), low risk of income disruption (so forbearance/IDR aren't needed as safety nets), and rate savings 2%+ to justify giving up federal protections. Anything less, keep federal loans.
conceptChoices: You want a lower rate (no other considerations)
ALL of these: stable high income, no public service plans, no risk of needing hardship pauses, and a meaningful (2%+) rate reduction
You're in your first job after graduation
You have less than $20k in loans
correctConceptChoice: ALL of these: stable high income, no public service plans, no risk of needing hardship pauses, and a meaningful (2%+) rate reduction

promptTemplate: On a $50k loan, refinancing saves you 1% in interest ($5k over 10 years). But you'd forfeit PSLF eligibility worth potentially $40k of forgiveness. The math says...
explanationTemplate: Even if PSLF eligibility is only 50% probable in your career path (you might leave public service), expected PSLF value is $20k. Compare to guaranteed $5k in rate savings — PSLF still wins by 4×. The math only favors refi when PSLF is essentially impossible (high earner in private sector with no public service interest).
conceptChoices: Refi wins — $5k saved is guaranteed; PSLF is uncertain
PSLF wins — potential $40k forgiveness vastly exceeds $5k interest savings even when discounted for uncertainty
They're equivalent — go with whichever feels better
Refi wins — federal protections aren't worth anything
correctConceptChoice: PSLF wins — potential $40k forgiveness vastly exceeds $5k interest savings even when discounted for uncertainty

promptTemplate: Your RSU grant vests {{sharesVested}} shares this quarter. Current share price is ${{sharePrice}}. What gross income is added to your W-2 from this vest?
explanationTemplate: Gross income added = {{sharesVested}} shares × ${{sharePrice}} = ${{answer}}. RSUs are taxed as ordinary income at vest (per IRS Pub 525) at THAT day's share price — not at the original grant price.

promptTemplate: You vest {{sharesVested}} shares at ${{sharePrice}}. Your combined marginal tax rate (federal + state + FICA Medicare) is {{marginalRate}}%. Net cash equivalent after tax?
explanationTemplate: Gross = {{sharesVested}} × ${{sharePrice}}. Net = gross × (1 − {{marginalRate}}%) = ${{answer}}. The IRS treats the vest as ordinary W-2 income (per IRS Pub 525) — same rate as your salary.

promptTemplate: Your employer withholds RSU taxes at the IRS supplemental rate of 22%. You're actually in the {{marginalRate}}% combined marginal bracket. On an RSU vest worth ${{vestValue}}, how much extra tax will you owe at filing?
explanationTemplate: Extra owed = vest × (your rate − 22%) = ${{vestValue}} × ({{marginalRate}}% − 22%) = ${{answer}}. The IRS supplemental withholding rate of 22% (per IRS Pub 15) is too low for high earners. Set aside the gap or you'll owe at filing.

promptTemplate: You receive an RSU grant of {{totalShares}} shares with a standard 4-year vest (25% per year, after a 1-year cliff). The stock is currently ${{sharePrice}}. What's the value of YEAR-1 vest at today's price?
explanationTemplate: Year-1 vest = 25% of {{totalShares}} = (total ÷ 4) shares × ${{sharePrice}} = ${{answer}}. Standard tech-industry vest schedule: 1-year cliff, then 25% per year (or quarterly equivalents). Each tranche is taxed at THAT date's share price.

promptTemplate: When are RSUs taxed?
explanationTemplate: RSUs are taxed AT VEST as ordinary income on the share price that day (per IRS Pub 525). When you later SELL, only the gain (or loss) above the vest-date price is a capital event. People often confuse this with stock options (ISOs / NSOs), which have different rules. Selling RSUs immediately at vest locks in the value at zero capital-gains exposure.
conceptChoices: At vest, as ordinary income at the current share price
At grant, when the RSU agreement is signed
At sale only, as a capital gain
Half at vest, half at sale
correctConceptChoice: At vest, as ordinary income at the current share price

promptTemplate: You contribute ${{contribution}} to your ESPP over a 6-month offering period at a {{discount}}% discount (qualified plan under IRC § 423). If you sell immediately at the same price you bought, how much do you net (gross gain, ignoring tax)?
explanationTemplate: Gain = contribution × discount / (100 − discount). At {{discount}}% discount on ${{contribution}}: gain = ${{answer}}. The math: you pay 85¢ for every $1 of stock, then sell at $1, so the 15¢ on each 85¢ = ~17.6% return.

promptTemplate: Your ESPP has a 6-month offering period with a 15% discount. If you quick-flip on purchase day, what's the approximate ANNUALIZED return on the contribution cycling through (ignoring tax)?
explanationTemplate: Per-period gain = 15 ÷ 85 = ~17.6%. Annualized: 2 cycles per year × 17.6% ≈ 35-38% effective annual return (compounding makes it slightly higher). This is why ESPP quick-flips are considered near-guaranteed money. The math is identical whether the stock goes up, down, or sideways during the period — the discount alone delivers the return.

promptTemplate: Your ESPP has a {{discount}}% discount with lookback. Stock was ${{startPrice}} at the start of the offering period and ${{endPrice}} at the end. You contributed ${{contribution}}. Purchase price uses LOWER of the two minus {{discount}}%. What's your gross gain if you sell immediately at the end-of-period price?
explanationTemplate: Purchase price = min(start, end) × 85%. Shares = contribution ÷ purchase price. Sell at end price → gross gain = shares × (end price − purchase price) = ${{answer}}. When the stock rises during the period, the lookback turns a great deal into a spectacular one — the discount stacks on top of the run-up.

promptTemplate: You're choosing between contributing $5,000 to a 15%-discount ESPP (quick-flip) vs investing $5,000 in an S&P 500 index fund. Same 6-month window. The ESPP delivers ~17.6% guaranteed; the S&P expected return is ~10%/year (~5% over 6 months). Which is better PURELY on expected return?
explanationTemplate: ESPP guaranteed ~17.6% beats S&P expected ~5% by a factor of ~3.5×, and the ESPP return is contractual (it's the discount math), not market-dependent. Standard advice for anyone with ESPP access: max it AND quick-flip, then invest the proceeds in the index fund. You capture both returns.
conceptChoices: ESPP, by a wide margin (17.6% guaranteed vs ~5% expected)
Index fund — diversified, less concentration risk
They're equivalent — both around 17%
Index fund — long-term tax treatment is better
correctConceptChoice: ESPP, by a wide margin (17.6% guaranteed vs ~5% expected)

promptTemplate: Your ESPP is a qualified plan (IRC § 423). For a 'qualifying disposition' that gets favorable long-term capital gains treatment on the discount portion, how long must you hold the shares?
explanationTemplate: Qualifying disposition under IRC § 423: at least 2 years from GRANT (start of offering period) AND 1 year from PURCHASE. If you sell before either window: 'disqualifying disposition' — the discount portion is ordinary income, not capital gains. For 6-month offering periods, both windows usually clear at 'hold for ~18 months from purchase.' Worth doing only if you'd hold the stock anyway — locking in the 17.6% via quick-flip + diversifying often beats waiting for the tax break.
conceptChoices: 2 years from grant + 1 year from purchase
1 year from purchase only
6 months from purchase
5 years from grant
correctConceptChoice: 2 years from grant + 1 year from purchase

promptTemplate: Your credit card has a ${{creditLimit}} limit. Your balance at statement close is ${{balanceAtStatement}}. What utilization % gets reported to the credit bureaus?
explanationTemplate: Utilization = balance ÷ limit × 100 = {{answer}}%. Credit bureaus see the balance as of STATEMENT CLOSE date, not the due date. Goal: keep this under 30% per card, ideally under 10% for the strongest score impact (payment history + utilization are 65% of FICO; per FICO score factor weights).

promptTemplate: Your credit card has a ${{creditLimit}} limit. To keep reported utilization at or under {{targetPct}}%, what's the maximum balance you can have at statement close?
explanationTemplate: Max balance at statement close = limit × target% = ${{creditLimit}} × {{targetPct}}% = ${{answer}}. Pay anything above this BEFORE the statement closes (not just before the due date) — that's the trick most people miss. The grace period (per CARD Act / Reg Z) only protects you from interest, not utilization reporting.

promptTemplate: Your card has a $5,000 limit. You charge $4,500 on Sep 14. Statement closes Sep 15. You pay the $4,500 in full on Oct 10 (the due date). What utilization gets reported to the bureaus for that cycle?
explanationTemplate: 90%. Credit bureaus see the balance as of the STATEMENT CLOSE (Sep 15), not as of payment (Oct 10). Paying by the due date saves you from interest, but the high-utilization snapshot already got reported. To prevent: pay BEFORE the statement closes, even partially — push the closing balance below 30% of the limit.
conceptChoices: 90% (balance at statement close was $4,500)
0% (paid in full before due date)
10% ($500 reported because rest was paid)
45% (halfway since paid mid-cycle)
correctConceptChoice: 90% (balance at statement close was $4,500)

promptTemplate: Which date determines the credit utilization that gets reported to the three credit bureaus?
explanationTemplate: STATEMENT CLOSE date — that's when the issuer snapshots your balance and reports it to Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion. The DUE DATE (typically 21-25 days later, per CARD Act / Reg Z grace period) only matters for whether you pay interest. To optimize utilization for FICO: pay BEFORE the statement closes.
conceptChoices: Statement close date — the day the balance is snapshotted and reported
Payment due date — the deadline to avoid interest
The first of each month, regardless of cycle
The day you make a purchase
correctConceptChoice: Statement close date — the day the balance is snapshotted and reported

promptTemplate: You have two credit cards: Card A with a ${{limitA}} limit and ${{balanceA}} at statement close. Card B with a ${{limitB}} limit and ${{balanceB}} at statement close. What's your AGGREGATE utilization across both cards?
explanationTemplate: Aggregate = total balance ÷ total limit × 100 = (${{balanceA}} + ${{balanceB}}) ÷ (${{limitA}} + ${{limitB}}) × 100 = {{answer}}%. FICO weighs BOTH per-card AND aggregate utilization. A high per-card utilization (even with low aggregate) still hurts your score. Keep both metrics under 30%.

promptTemplate: When does most employer-sponsored open enrollment happen for a typical US worker?
explanationTemplate: Most employer open enrollment runs late October through mid-November for a plan year starting January 1. (ACA Marketplace open enrollment is similar: Nov 1 through Jan 15, per Healthcare.gov.) Outside the window, you can only change benefits with a qualifying life event (marriage, baby, divorce, job loss).
conceptChoices: Late October through mid-November, for benefits starting January 1
Any time during the year
January, after the new year starts
Aligned with your employment anniversary
correctConceptChoice: Late October through mid-November, for benefits starting January 1

scenarioTemplate: You're healthy, rarely see a doctor, and have $5,000 in emergency savings. Plan A: $260/mo premium, $500 deductible. Plan B: $95/mo premium, $4,500 deductible.
promptTemplate: Which plan is the smarter pick, and why?
explanationTemplate: Premiums are paid no matter what; the deductible is only paid if you have a claim. Plan B's premiums cost about $1,980/yr less ($1,140 vs $3,120) — near-guaranteed savings in a low-usage year. The trade-off is risk: Plan B's worst case is the $4,500 deductible, but your $5,000 emergency fund covers it. The rule: a high-deductible / low-premium plan wins when you (1) use little care AND (2) can comfortably cover the deductible. If either isn't true, lean toward the lower deductible.
conceptChoices: Plan B — you pocket about $1,980/yr in lower premiums, and your $5,000 savings can absorb the higher deductible if something goes wrong
Plan A — a lower deductible is always the safer financial choice
Plan B — but only because the deductible never matters when you're healthy
Plan A — paying more in premiums guarantees a lower total cost
correctConceptChoice: Plan B — you pocket about $1,980/yr in lower premiums, and your $5,000 savings can absorb the higher deductible if something goes wrong

scenarioTemplate: You've already met your deductible this year; your plan then pays 80% (you pay 20% coinsurance). You need an MRI. In-network, it's billed at $1,200. An out-of-network imaging center quotes a $700 cash price.
promptTemplate: Which option costs you less — and what's the hidden benefit?
explanationTemplate: With your deductible already met, in-network you pay 20% of the negotiated $1,200 = $240. The $700 cash price looks lower than the $1,200 sticker, but you'd pay the full $700 — and cash paid to an out-of-network provider usually does NOT count toward your deductible or out-of-pocket max. In-network is cheaper now ($240) AND moves you toward the OOP max, after which the plan pays 100%.
conceptChoices: In-network — you pay 20% of $1,200 = $240, well below the $700 cash price, and it counts toward your out-of-pocket max
Out-of-network cash — $700 is a lower price than the $1,200 sticker
They cost about the same once you factor in coinsurance
Out-of-network — paying cash always avoids insurance hassles and saves money
correctConceptChoice: In-network — you pay 20% of $1,200 = $240, well below the $700 cash price, and it counts toward your out-of-pocket max

scenarioTemplate: You're healthy and expect about one doctor visit this year. Your employer offers an HSA-qualified HDHP ($1,700 deductible) at $80/mo and seeds $1,000 into your HSA — or a PPO ($500 deductible) at $230/mo.
promptTemplate: For someone who rarely needs care, which plan is usually the better financial deal?
explanationTemplate: For low expected usage, compare the near-certain costs: the HDHP's premiums are $1,800/yr cheaper ($960 vs $2,760), and the employer's $1,000 HSA contribution is free money. The HSA adds a triple tax advantage (pre-tax in, tax-free growth, tax-free for medical). The PPO's lower deductible only pays off with heavy usage — which you don't have. HDHP/HSA eligibility requires the IRS-qualified plan (2026 minimum deductible $1,700 self, per IRS Rev Proc 2025-19).
conceptChoices: The HDHP — its premiums cost $1,800/yr less, the employer adds $1,000 to your HSA, and HSA money is triple-tax-advantaged
The PPO — the lower deductible saves more money for everyone
The HDHP — but only if you never see a doctor at all
It's a coin flip; deductibles and premiums always cancel out
correctConceptChoice: The HDHP — its premiums cost $1,800/yr less, the employer adds $1,000 to your HSA, and HSA money is triple-tax-advantaged

promptTemplate: To make HSA contributions during open enrollment, what's required?
explanationTemplate: HSA eligibility requires enrollment in an HSA-qualified HDHP (per IRS Rev Proc 2025-19, 2026 minimum deductibles: $1,700 self / $3,400 family). You CANNOT contribute to an HSA if you're enrolled in a non-HDHP plan, in Medicare, or claimed as a dependent on someone else's tax return. The HDHP / HSA combination is the only way to get the HSA's triple tax advantage.
conceptChoices: Enrolled in an HSA-qualified HDHP plan
Any health plan offered by your employer
Enrollment in a Marketplace plan only
FSA enrollment first, then HSA
correctConceptChoice: Enrolled in an HSA-qualified HDHP plan

promptTemplate: What's the 2026 contribution cap for a Dependent Care FSA (DCFSA), per family?
explanationTemplate: $7,500 per household per year ($3,750 if married filing separately) — raised from $5,000 by OBBBA 2025, the first increase since 1986. Used for childcare, after-school care, summer day camp for kids under 13 (or care for a disabled spouse/dependent). At a 22-32% bracket, the DCFSA saves $1,650-2,400/yr in taxes — often the single highest-ROI open-enrollment election for parents.
conceptChoices: $3,400 (same as Health FSA)
$5,000 (the old pre-2026 cap)

promptTemplate: Which account is 'use-it-or-lose-it' by default — meaning unspent funds at year-end are typically forfeited?
explanationTemplate: FSAs are use-it-or-lose-it (per IRS). Employers can offer one of two relief mechanisms: a 2.5-month grace period to spend prior-year funds, OR a limited rollover (~$680 for 2026, per IRS Rev Proc 2025-32). HSAs have no use-it-or-lose-it rule — funds roll over indefinitely and can be invested. This is the single biggest difference between the two.
conceptChoices: FSA — unspent funds are typically forfeited at year-end
HSA — must spend annually
Both — they're effectively the same
Neither — both roll over indefinitely
correctConceptChoice: FSA — unspent funds are typically forfeited at year-end

promptTemplate: Your employer offers free group life insurance equal to 1× salary, plus the option to buy supplemental coverage (2-5× salary) at pre-tax rates. When does supplemental coverage usually make sense?
explanationTemplate: Supplemental life via employer makes sense when you have dependents (kids / spouse who relies on your income) AND the supplemental rate is below what individual term-life would cost. For most healthy 30-somethings, individual 20-30 year term-life is cheaper than employer supplemental, but for older workers or those with health issues, employer group coverage often beats individual underwriting. If you have no dependents, skip it.
conceptChoices: When you have dependents (kids/spouse) and the rate beats individual term-life
Always — it's free pre-tax money
Only after retirement age
Only if you have less than $50K in savings
correctConceptChoice: When you have dependents (kids/spouse) and the rate beats individual term-life

promptTemplate: In 2026, what's the maximum employee elective deferral to a Roth 401(k)?
explanationTemplate: $24,500 for 2026 (per IRS Notice 2025-67). This cap is SHARED with the Traditional 401(k) at the same employer — you can't max both for $49,000 total. Workers 50+ get an additional $8,000 catch-up (ages 60-63 get an $11,250 super catch-up instead, per SECURE 2.0). The IRA limit ($7,500) is separate and additive.
conceptChoices: $24,500 — shared with Traditional 401(k) at the same employer
$7,500 — same as the IRA cap
$32,000 — combined with the IRA
$72,000 — including employer match
correctConceptChoice: $24,500 — shared with Traditional 401(k) at the same employer

promptTemplate: You contribute 100% to your Roth 401(k). Your employer offers a 50% match up to 6% of salary. Which bucket does the match land in?
explanationTemplate: Employer matches ALWAYS go into the Traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) bucket, regardless of where your own elective contributions go. SECURE 2.0 allows plans to OFFER a Roth match option starting 2024, but the default + most plans still send the match pre-tax. This means your match grows tax-deferred and is taxed at withdrawal (like a Traditional 401(k)) — even if your own contributions are Roth.
conceptChoices: Traditional 401(k) (pre-tax) — taxed at withdrawal
Roth 401(k) — matches your election
A separate 'match' account with its own rules
Roth IRA — added to your individual account
correctConceptChoice: Traditional 401(k) (pre-tax) — taxed at withdrawal

promptTemplate: Which of these accounts has an INCOME PHASEOUT that prevents high earners from contributing directly?
explanationTemplate: Roth IRA only. 2026 phaseout (per IRS Notice 2025-67): $153K–$168K for single, $242K–$252K for MFJ — direct contributions phase out and stop at the upper bound. Roth 401(k) has NO income phaseout, so high earners excluded from Roth IRA can still get Roth tax treatment via their employer plan. Traditional 401(k) and Traditional IRA also have no income cap on contributions (Traditional IRA has a separate phaseout on deductibility, not on contribution).
conceptChoices: Roth IRA only — $153K single / $242K MFJ start in 2026
Roth 401(k) and Roth IRA — both have phaseouts
Traditional 401(k) — limits contributions above $200K
All three Roth-flavored accounts have phaseouts
correctConceptChoice: Roth IRA only — $153K single / $242K MFJ start in 2026

promptTemplate: You're under 50, earning $90K single in 2026. What's your MAXIMUM combined annual contribution capacity across a 401(k) (any mix Roth + Traditional) and an IRA (any mix Roth + Traditional)?
explanationTemplate: $32,000. That's $24,500 elective deferral cap (401k, any Roth/Trad mix) + $7,500 IRA cap (any Roth/Trad mix). The caps are independent — separate buckets, not combined. At 50+, add $8,000 401(k) catch-up + $1,100 IRA catch-up → $41,100 max. Employer match is on top of these limits but counts toward the $72,000 (2026) overall §415 cap (per IRS).
conceptChoices: $24,500 — IRA and 401(k) share the cap
$7,500 — IRA only since income is below phaseout
$72,000 — including employer match

promptTemplate: Which of these accounts has NO required minimum distributions (RMDs) during the original owner's lifetime?
explanationTemplate: Roth IRA. RMD rules (per IRS / SECURE 2.0): Traditional 401(k) and Traditional IRA have RMDs starting at age 73 (rising to 75 in 2033). Roth 401(k) HAD RMDs at age 73 historically, but SECURE 2.0 eliminated them starting in 2024 — bringing it in line with Roth IRA. So only Roth accounts (both IRA and 401(k)) are now RMD-free during the owner's lifetime. The pre-2024 rule was a common 'Roth IRA but not Roth 401(k)' distinction — that's now obsolete.
conceptChoices: Roth IRA (and Roth 401(k) post-SECURE 2.0)
Traditional IRA only
Traditional 401(k) only
All retirement accounts have RMDs at age 73
correctConceptChoice: Roth IRA (and Roth 401(k) post-SECURE 2.0)

promptTemplate: You have ${{totalAmount}} to invest. Instead of lump-summing, you DCA evenly over 12 months. Expected market return during that year is {{annualReturn}}%. Approximate cash drag — the foregone return on the dollars still sitting in cash on average?
explanationTemplate: Cash drag ≈ total × annual return ÷ 2 = ${{totalAmount}} × {{annualReturn}}% ÷ 2 = ${{answer}}. Why ÷ 2? When you DCA evenly over 12 months, the dollars going in last month earn ~1 month of return; the first-month dollars earn ~12 months. On average, contributions earn ~half a year of return — vs lump-sum where every dollar earns the full year. The difference is the math premium of lump-sum. Behavioral DCA premium (guaranteed deployment) usually outweighs this in practice.

promptTemplate: Quick screen: an offer is ${{hourly1099}}/hr as a 1099 contractor. Using the rough rule that 1099 hourly × 0.70 ≈ W-2 take-home equivalent (after SE tax + missing benefits + missing PTO, net of the QBI deduction), what W-2 hourly does this approximately match?
explanationTemplate: 1099 × 0.70 = ${{hourly1099}} × 0.70 = ${{answer}}. The ~30% haircut covers employer FICA half (~7.65%), missing employer-sponsored health insurance (~7-10% of base), missing 401(k) match (~3-6%), missing PTO (~5-8%), and self-funded disability/life — partially offset by the 20% QBI deduction (permanent post-OBBBA). Quick screen — if your 1099 offer's W-2-equivalent is below your current W-2 pay, it's not actually a raise.

promptTemplate: You currently earn ${{currentW2Hourly}}/hr W-2 with full benefits. What 1099 hourly rate would you need to roughly break even on take-home? Use the 1099 × 0.70 ≈ W-2 take-home rule.
explanationTemplate: Solve W-2 = 1099 × 0.70 for 1099: 1099 needed = W-2 ÷ 0.70 = ${{currentW2Hourly}} ÷ 0.70 ≈ ${{answer}}/hr. Anything less than this 1099 rate is a real pay cut. If you have access to spouse's health insurance or qualify for ACA Marketplace subsidies, the multiplier shrinks (closer to 0.78-0.85).

promptTemplate: On ${{annual1099}} of 1099 income, what's your effective self-employment tax? Use the IRS Schedule SE effective rate of ~14.13% (15.3% applied to 92.35% of earnings, per IRS).
explanationTemplate: SE tax = annual × 14.13% = ${{annual1099}} × 14.13% ≈ ${{answer}}. This is on top of federal income tax + state tax. A W-2 employee's employer pays half of FICA (7.65%) on their behalf; a 1099 contractor pays both halves. The 92.35% factor (per IRS Schedule SE) deducts the employer-equivalent half before computing SE tax — bringing the effective rate down from 15.3% to 14.13%.

promptTemplate: Offer A: ${{w2Hourly}}/hr W-2 (2,080 hours) plus benefits worth ~$12,000/year (health + 401k match + PTO). Offer B: ${{c1099Hourly}}/hr 1099, no benefits. What's the total-comp gap (Offer A total comp minus Offer B gross)?
explanationTemplate: Offer A total comp = ${{w2Hourly}} × 2,080 + $12,000 benefits. Offer B gross = ${{c1099Hourly}} × 2,080. Gap (A − B) = ${{answer}}. Negative means B's headline rate beats A's total comp; positive means A wins despite the lower headline. Always compute both ways — many 'higher rate' 1099 offers lose on total comp.

promptTemplate: Which of these is NOT a benefit you'd lose by switching from W-2 to 1099?
explanationTemplate: Your contributions to YOUR own retirement account aren't 'lost' — you'd just switch from a Traditional/Roth 401(k) to a Solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA. What you DO lose: the employer FICA half (~7.65%, becomes self-employment tax instead), the employer 401(k) match (free 3-6% of salary), employer-sponsored health insurance (~$6-8K/yr value), and paid time off (~5-8% of salary in unbilled days). All of those have to be self-funded from your gross 1099 rate.
conceptChoices: Your own retirement contributions — you can still open a Solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA
The employer 401(k) match
Employer-paid half of FICA (~7.65%)
Paid time off
correctConceptChoice: Your own retirement contributions — you can still open a Solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA

promptTemplate: Your employer's 401(k) match has a 4-year graded vesting schedule (25% per year). You've accumulated ${{totalMatch}} in employer match and you've worked there for {{yearsServed}} full years. How much of the match is vested?
explanationTemplate: Vested = total × min(years ÷ 4, 1.0) = ${{totalMatch}} × ({{yearsServed}}/4) = ${{answer}}. Graded vesting per IRC § 411(a)(2)(B). Each completed year of service vests an additional 25% on a standard 4-year schedule. Your own contributions are always 100% vested from day one.

promptTemplate: Your employer uses a 3-year cliff vesting schedule on the 401(k) match. You leave after 2 years and 10 months with $8,000 of accumulated employer match. How much do you vest?
explanationTemplate: $0. Cliff vesting is binary (per IRC § 411(a)(2)(A)) — 0% before the cliff date, 100% after. You forfeit the entire $8,000 by leaving 2 months before the 3-year cliff. Staying another 2 months unlocks the full $8K — a clear case where checking your vesting schedule before changing jobs matters.
conceptChoices: $0 — cliff vesting is binary; you forfeit the entire match
$5,333 — pro-rated to 2 yr 10 mo of 3 yrs
$8,000 — the match is always yours
$2,667 — only year 3 forfeits
correctConceptChoice: $0 — cliff vesting is binary; you forfeit the entire match

promptTemplate: You have ${{totalMatch}} accumulated employer match on a {{vestYears}}-year graded vesting schedule. You leave after {{yearsServed}} full years. How much match is FORFEITED (left behind with the employer)?
explanationTemplate: Vested % = years ÷ vestYears. Forfeited = total × (1 − vested%) = ${{totalMatch}} × (1 − {{yearsServed}}/{{vestYears}}) = ${{answer}}. The forfeited amount is real cash that goes back to the plan (or stays with the employer per the plan document). Always check whether staying another 6-12 months captures another vesting tier before accepting a new offer.

promptTemplate: On a 4-year graded vesting schedule (25%/yr), you've accumulated ${{totalMatch}} in employer match and you're at 2 years 8 months of service. If you stay another {{extraMonths}} months to hit the next 25% milestone, how much ADDITIONAL match do you capture (vs leaving today)?
explanationTemplate: Currently vested at 2 full years → 50%. Hitting the next 25% milestone bumps you to 75% = additional 25% × ${{totalMatch}} = ${{answer}}. This is real cash that's captured by waiting through the milestone — the question for a new-job decision is whether the new offer's signing bonus / salary delta exceeds this captured amount. Often it doesn't.

promptTemplate: You have two job offers with the same total comp. Offer A vests its 401(k) match on a 3-year CLIFF schedule. Offer B vests on a 4-year GRADED schedule (25% per year). You're not sure you'll stay 3+ years. Which vesting schedule is friendlier to your match if you leave early?
explanationTemplate: Graded vesting wins on the downside. With graded, leaving at 18 months captures ~25-37.5% of the match (depending on month counting); with a 3-year cliff, leaving at 18 months captures 0%. Cliff schedules are better for the employer (retention through the cliff date); graded is friendlier to employees who might leave early. If you're confident you'll stay 5+ years, the difference disappears — both fully vest.
conceptChoices: Offer B's graded schedule — at least some vesting accumulates each year
Offer A's cliff schedule — bigger lump sum at vest
They're identical from the employee perspective
Cliff is better because it doesn't require partial calculations
correctConceptChoice: Offer B's graded schedule — at least some vesting accumulates each year

promptTemplate: You're building your first emergency fund, currently $400 saved, working toward a $1,000 starter EF (per the r/personalfinance Order of Operations). Where should this money live right now?
explanationTemplate: At sub-$1,000 balances, liquidity matters more than yield. Your checking account or a basic savings sub-account at the same bank is fine. Opening a separate HYSA for $400 is friction without real reward (~$14/yr at 4.5% APY vs ~$1.50 at 0.01% — both negligible). Once you cross $1K, move to a HYSA.
conceptChoices: Checking account or basic savings — liquidity beats yield at this size
Open a HYSA immediately, even for $400
Buy short-term T-bills
Index fund — start growing it now
correctConceptChoice: Checking account or basic savings — liquidity beats yield at this size

promptTemplate: Your full emergency fund is $20,000 (6 months of essentials). It's currently in a big-bank checking account paying 0.01% APY. What's the right home for it?
explanationTemplate: A high-yield savings account (HYSA) at 4-5% APY (FDIC-insured, per FDIC, up to $250K). Moving $20K from 0.01% to 4.5% earns you ~$900/year in passive interest — same liquidity, same FDIC protection. Don't lock it in a CD (early-withdrawal penalty defeats the purpose), don't put it in an index fund (could be down when you need it).
conceptChoices: HYSA at 4-5% APY — same liquidity, ~$900/yr more interest
Keep it in checking — easier access
12-month CD at 5%+ APY
Index fund — beat inflation
correctConceptChoice: HYSA at 4-5% APY — same liquidity, ~$900/yr more interest

promptTemplate: Your emergency fund has grown to $320,000 (you've kept saving past the 6-month target during high-income years). FDIC insures $250,000 per depositor per bank. What's the right move?
explanationTemplate: Split across at least 2 FDIC-insured banks (e.g. $250K at one, $70K at another), OR move a portion into short-term US Treasury bills via TreasuryDirect — T-bills carry the full faith and credit of the US Treasury (no banking-system risk, no FDIC limit), pay similar yield, and are state-tax-free. Both approaches keep your full balance protected. Many fintech HYSAs use a 'sweep network' to spread deposits across multiple partner banks invisibly — that also works.
conceptChoices: Split across 2+ FDIC-insured banks OR move excess to short-term T-bills
Leave it all at one bank — $250K limit is only a guideline
Move it to a brokerage account
Open a CD — higher yield than HYSA
correctConceptChoice: Split across 2+ FDIC-insured banks OR move excess to short-term T-bills

promptTemplate: Which of these is the WRONG place to keep your emergency fund?
explanationTemplate: Your 401(k) is the wrong place. Accessing it early triggers ordinary income tax + a 10% early-withdrawal penalty (per IRS, with limited exceptions for hardship). On a $10K withdrawal at a 24% bracket, you'd net only ~$6,600 — a 34% haircut on emergency cash you'll urgently need. The other options preserve liquidity and value: HYSA (liquid, insured), checking (liquid, no yield), even a brokerage settlement account (liquid in 1-2 days, money-market fund yield). An EF must be both liquid AND value-preserving when emergencies hit.
conceptChoices: Your 401(k) — early withdrawal triggers tax + 10% penalty
A high-yield savings account
Checking account
Brokerage settlement / money-market account
correctConceptChoice: Your 401(k) — early withdrawal triggers tax + 10% penalty

promptTemplate: A 12-month CD offers 5.0% APY. Your HYSA offers 4.5% APY. Should you move your full emergency fund into the CD for the extra 0.5%?
explanationTemplate: No — early-withdrawal penalty on a CD typically costs 3-6 months of interest, which on a 1-year CD wipes out most of the gain you'd capture if you actually do need the money mid-year. The whole point of an EF is being available when emergencies happen. Compromise option: keep your full EF in HYSA, and put any 'beyond-EF' savings (the buffer you don't actually need for 6 months) in a no-penalty CD or short T-bill ladder. The 0.5% APY difference on a $20K EF is $100/year — not worth the liquidity risk.
conceptChoices: No — early-withdrawal penalty defeats the purpose of an emergency fund
Yes — 0.5% extra is meaningful on $20K+
Yes — most CDs let you withdraw without penalty
Yes — but only if you split the EF half HYSA, half CD
correctConceptChoice: No — early-withdrawal penalty defeats the purpose of an emergency fund

promptTemplate: You're buying a ${{purchasePrice}} home with {{downPct}}% down. Using the quick rule that cash-to-close ≈ down payment + 5% of purchase price (covers closing costs, escrow, reserves), approximately how much cash do you need at the closing table?
explanationTemplate: Cash to close ≈ price × (down% + 5%) = ${{purchasePrice}} × ({{downPct}}% + 5%) = ${{answer}}. The 5% covers loan origination (~1%), title + escrow (~1%), prepaid property tax + insurance (~2%), and inspection / appraisal / recording. CFPB Consumer Closing Costs research puts the typical range at 2-5% of purchase price. Plus $2-3K for moving and setup — not on the settlement statement but you still need the cash.

promptTemplate: On a ${{purchasePrice}} home with 10% down, what's the LOAN ORIGINATION fee at the typical 1% of loan amount?
