explanationTemplate: Loan amount = price × 90% = ${{purchasePrice}} × 0.9. Origination fee = loan × 1% = ${{answer}}. This is one of the largest closing-cost line items. Some lenders advertise 'no origination fee' but typically bake it into a slightly higher rate; compare APRs, not just rates.

promptTemplate: You're buying a $400,000 home with 20% down (avoiding PMI). Using the quick rule: cash needed at closing ≈ down + 5% of price + $3K moving. What's your total cash requirement before move-in?
explanationTemplate: Down: $80K. Closing-cost padding (5% of $400K): $20K. Moving / setup: $3K. Total: $103K. The 20% down saves PMI (~$150/month on $320K loan) but the upfront cash hurdle is meaningful — many buyers underestimate by $20-30K because they anchor only on the down payment.
conceptChoices: $103,000 ($80K down + $20K closing + $3K moving)
$80,000 (the down payment)
$95,000 ($80K + $15K closing only)
$120,000 ($80K + $40K closing — closing costs are 10%)
correctConceptChoice: $103,000 ($80K down + $20K closing + $3K moving)

promptTemplate: A ${{purchasePrice}} home with {{downPct}}% down. Estimate the total cash needed BEFORE move-in (closing + moving / setup combined): down + 5% closing + ${{movingCash}} moving / setup.
explanationTemplate: Total = price × (down% + 5%) + moving = ${{purchasePrice}} × ({{downPct}}% + 5%) + ${{movingCash}} = ${{answer}}. The moving / setup line catches even buyers who budgeted closing costs — utility deposits, immediate furniture, light fixtures, appliances, cleaning, and grocery restock add up faster than expected.

promptTemplate: Which of these is NOT a typical closing-cost component on a US home purchase?
explanationTemplate: Property tax for the FULL upcoming year is not paid at closing — you prepay 2-6 months of property tax + insurance into an escrow account (per typical lender requirements). Full-year property tax is paid by the escrow account in installments as bills come due. The other line items ARE typical closing costs (per CFPB Consumer Closing Costs research): origination, title insurance, appraisal/inspection, and recording.
conceptChoices: Full-year property tax bill — only 2-6 months go into prepaid escrow
Loan origination fee (typically ~1% of loan amount)
Title insurance + recording fees
Appraisal + inspection
correctConceptChoice: Full-year property tax bill — only 2-6 months go into prepaid escrow

promptTemplate: A new job offers a ${{nominalRaise}} raise. The move increases your rent by ${{rentDelta}}/month. Ignoring state-tax change, what's the REAL annual income change?
explanationTemplate: Real change = raise − (rent delta × 12) = ${{nominalRaise}} − ${{rentDelta}} × 12 = ${{answer}}. Positive means the raise still nets a real income increase; negative means rent eats more than the raise (the move is actually a pay cut despite the higher salary). Add state-tax delta and commute / sales-tax changes for the full picture, but housing usually dominates.

promptTemplate: Your new offer has a ${{nominalRaise}} raise. Your new city's rent is ${{rentDelta}}/month higher than your current. How many months of higher rent does it take to eat the raise entirely?
explanationTemplate: Months = raise ÷ rent delta = ${{nominalRaise}} ÷ ${{rentDelta}} = {{answer}} months. If this number is under 12, the rent jump eats the entire raise inside the first year. Even at 12-18 months, the after-tax math typically turns the move into a net pay cut once you add state-tax and commute deltas.

promptTemplate: Moving from a state with 0% income tax to one with {{newStateRate}}% effective. New salary is ${{newSalary}}. What's the annual increase in state income tax owed?
explanationTemplate: State tax delta = salary × rate = ${{newSalary}} × {{newStateRate}}% = ${{answer}}. Moving from TX/FL/WA/NV (no income tax) to CA (~9.3% effective) on a $120K salary costs ~$11K/yr in additional state tax. Combined with rent + cost-of-living, no-tax-state to high-tax-state moves frequently cost more than they pay.

promptTemplate: Current job: ${{currentSalary}} in a no-state-tax state, $1,500/mo rent. Considering a move to NY (9.3% effective combined NY state + NYC city tax on top of federal), where rent will be $3,000/mo. What salary do you need in NY to roughly break even on real income?
explanationTemplate: Breakeven new salary ≈ current salary + (rent delta × 12) + (tax rate × new salary). Solving: newSalary × (1 − 9.3%) ≈ currentSalary + rent delta × 12, so newSalary ≈ (current + $18K) ÷ 0.907 ≈ ${{answer}}. The high-tax + high-rent combination means NY moves need roughly $30-50K of nominal raise just to stand still on real income.

scenarioTemplate: You currently earn $95,000 in Austin (0% state tax, $1,800/mo rent). You have a new offer for ${{newSalary}} in {{newCity}}.
promptTemplate: {{newCity}}: {{newCityStateRate}}% effective combined state+local tax, ${{newRent}}/mo rent. What's the REAL annual income change?
explanationTemplate: Real change = (newSalary − currentSalary) − (rent delta × 12) − (newSalary × state tax %). On ${{newSalary}} new salary, {{newCityStateRate}}% state tax, and ${{newRent}} rent vs $1,800 Austin: real change ≈ ${{answer}}. Negative means the move is a real pay cut despite the higher salary. Three-line subtraction is the fastest way to see it.

promptTemplate: Move-in cash on a $1,800/mo apartment (first + last + security): $5,400. Add the typical extras: ~$3,000 for a 1BR move (utilities setup + furniture + moving + restock). What's the total first-month TRUE cost?
explanationTemplate: $5,400 + $3,000 = $8,400. The rule-of-thumb $3,000 add-on covers utility setup deposits, immediate furniture/setup, moving, and grocery restock. A 1BR typically needs $3K of padding; larger places need more. The headline 'move-in cost' of $5,400 understates the real cash needed by ~55%.
conceptChoices: $8,400 ($5,400 rent-component + $3,000 add-ons)
$5,400 (rent-component move-in only)
$6,500 (small extras only)
$10,000+ (always more than expected)
correctConceptChoice: $8,400 ($5,400 rent-component + $3,000 add-ons)

promptTemplate: Quick rule: first-month padding ≈ $3,000 base + $1,000 per bedroom. For a {{bedrooms}}-bedroom apartment, what padding should you add to the rent-component move-in cost?
explanationTemplate: Padding = $3,000 base + $1,000 × {{bedrooms}} bedrooms = ${{answer}}. Larger places need more furniture, more rooms to set up, more grocery restock, and bigger movers. The rule is conservative — actual cost varies by how much you bring with you. Half of the padding (utility deposits, renters insurance prepaid annually) is refundable or pre-funded for future months, but the cash still has to clear upfront.

promptTemplate: Moving into a ${{monthlyRent}}/mo apartment, no broker fee, 1BR. Rent-component (first + last + security): ${{rentComponent}}. Adding utility setup ($400), movers ($700), mattress + setup ($800), and grocery restock ($300). What's the total first-month TRUE cost?
explanationTemplate: ${{rentComponent}} + $400 + $700 + $800 + $300 = ${{answer}}. The $2,200 of add-ons is conservative for a 1BR no-broker move; if you need furniture beyond a mattress, expect $1,500-3,000 in furniture alone. The rent-only move-in figure understates by 35-55% in most realistic moves.

promptTemplate: Moving into a ${{monthlyRent}}/mo apartment in a broker-fee city (NYC, Boston, parts of SF). Broker fee = 1 month's rent. Rent-component cash = first + last + security + broker = 4 × rent. Add ${{padding}} for utilities + furniture + moving + restock. Total first-month TRUE cost?
explanationTemplate: Rent-component (4 × ${{monthlyRent}}) + padding = ${{answer}}. Broker-fee cities have the highest first-month cash hurdle — a $3,000 NYC studio can easily require $15,000+ in cash before keys. As of 2024-25, NYC has banned tenant-paid broker fees on landlord-listed apartments (per NYC FARE Act), shifting the cost to landlords; check local rules before assuming you owe it.

promptTemplate: Which of these is most often UNDERESTIMATED by first-time movers when budgeting for a first apartment?
explanationTemplate: Utility setup and immediate household basics (mattress, kitchen, lighting, cleaning, garbage cans, shower curtain, etc.) typically run $1,500-3,000 for a first solo apartment — and they all need to clear in week one. New renters anchor on the rent-component move-in cash (first + last + security) and forget that an empty apartment is genuinely empty. The rent component is visible; the setup cost isn't.
conceptChoices: Utility setup + immediate household basics (mattress, kitchen, cleaning)
The security deposit (usually clearly communicated by the landlord)
First month's rent (the headline number)
Renters insurance (usually only $15-20/month)
correctConceptChoice: Utility setup + immediate household basics (mattress, kitchen, cleaning)

promptTemplate: Your EOB shows: total billed ${{billed}}, network adjustment ${{adjusted}}, insurance paid ${{insurancePaid}}. What's your patient responsibility according to the EOB?
explanationTemplate: Patient responsibility = billed − adjusted − insurance paid = ${{billed}} − ${{adjusted}} − ${{insurancePaid}} = ${{answer}}. This is the number you ACTUALLY owe. If the provider bill is higher than this, dispute it via your insurer's billing line — the provider may not have applied the network adjustment correctly.

promptTemplate: Provider bill says you owe ${{providerBill}}. EOB patient-responsibility line shows ${{eobOwed}}. How much is the provider over-charging (the amount you should dispute)?
explanationTemplate: Over-charge = provider bill − EOB patient responsibility = ${{providerBill}} − ${{eobOwed}} = ${{answer}}. Call the insurer's billing-dispute line (not the provider). Reference the EOB. The No Surprises Act of 2022 prohibits out-of-network billing in emergencies and at in-network facilities — common source of these gaps.

promptTemplate: You're uninsured. Hospital list price for a procedure is ${{listPrice}}. You ask for a cash-pay discount and they offer {{discountPct}}% off. What do you pay?
explanationTemplate: Cash price = list × (1 − discount%) = ${{listPrice}} × (1 − {{discountPct}}%) = ${{answer}}. US hospital list prices are essentially fiction. Uninsured / self-pay patients commonly negotiate 30-50% off via the hospital's financial-hardship or cash-pay program. Always ask before paying the bill as printed.

promptTemplate: What is an Explanation of Benefits (EOB)?
explanationTemplate: An EOB is a statement FROM YOUR INSURER (not the provider) showing how a claim was processed: what the provider billed, what insurance paid, what was adjusted off via the network rate, and what you owe (the 'patient responsibility' line). It's not a bill — it's the breakdown of how the claim was processed. The actual BILL comes separately from the provider. Compare the two: any gap is worth disputing.
conceptChoices: A statement from your insurer showing how a claim was processed (not a bill)
A bill from the provider — same thing as the invoice
A receipt for your copay
The insurance card you carry
correctConceptChoice: A statement from your insurer showing how a claim was processed (not a bill)

promptTemplate: Your provider bill arrives showing $3,200. Your EOB's patient-responsibility line shows $1,400. What should you do?
explanationTemplate: Call your insurer's billing-dispute line (number is on the EOB), not the provider. The insurer will work it out with the provider, who likely didn't apply the network adjustment. Filing a dispute auto-pauses collections for 30+ days while it's resolved. Paying the wrong $3,200 doesn't make the dispute easier — you'd have to claw back the overage later, which is harder. The 50-80% billing-error rate (per Consumer Reports + Medical Billing Advocates of America) is exactly why this routine matters.
conceptChoices: Call the insurer's billing-dispute line — provider likely didn't apply the network adjustment
Pay the $3,200 — provider knows the right amount
Pay the EOB's $1,400 amount without notifying anyone
Wait until collections starts and dispute then
correctConceptChoice: Call the insurer's billing-dispute line — provider likely didn't apply the network adjustment

promptTemplate: Your cashback card gives {{cashbackPct}}% back. You spend ${{monthlySpend}}/month on it. You pay statement balance in full each month (no interest). How much cashback do you earn per month?
explanationTemplate: Cashback = monthly spend × cashback% = ${{monthlySpend}} × {{cashbackPct}}% = ${{answer}}/month. Multiply by 12 for annual. THIS ONLY APPLIES if you pay statement balance in full. Carry a balance and the APR usually swamps the rewards (see other templates in this lesson).

promptTemplate: Same {{cashbackPct}}% cashback card. ${{monthlySpend}}/month spend. You're now carrying a ${{balance}} balance at {{apr}}% APR. What's your NET monthly result (rewards minus interest)?
explanationTemplate: Net = (spend × cashback%) − (balance × APR ÷ 1200) = (${{monthlySpend}} × {{cashbackPct}}%) − (${{balance}} × {{apr}}% ÷ 12) = ${{answer}}/month. Negative number means the rewards are NET LOSSES. The carried balance's monthly interest typically overwhelms any reasonable cashback rate. Pay off the balance before optimizing for rewards.

promptTemplate: You spend ${{monthlySpend}}/month on a {{cashbackPct}}% card. The card's APR is {{apr}}%. At what carried balance do your rewards exactly equal the monthly interest charge (the break-even balance)?
explanationTemplate: Break-even = monthly spend × cashback% × 12 ÷ APR = ${{monthlySpend}} × {{cashbackPct}}% × 12 ÷ {{apr}}% = ${{answer}}. Above this carried balance, rewards turn net-negative. Below it, rewards still win. For most US cashback cards, the break-even sits well under typical 'carried' balances — meaning anyone with a real revolving balance is losing money on the rewards card.

promptTemplate: You carry a $6,000 balance on your 2% cashback card at 24% APR. You spend $1,500/month and pay it down by only the minimum payment. How much are you losing PER YEAR on the 'rewards' card vs a 15% APR low-rewards card you could have instead?
explanationTemplate: Interest at 24% on $6K balance: $1,440/year. Interest at 15% on same $6K: $900/year. Annual difference: $540 saved by switching. Rewards on $1,500/mo × 2% × 12 = $360/year. So switching to the lower-APR card SAVES $540 but COSTS $360 in lost rewards — net $180/year better off. The marketing implication that 'rewards offset interest' is mathematically wrong when you carry a balance.
conceptChoices: About $180/year (interest saved by switching to a 15% APR card exceeds the lost rewards)
Nothing — the rewards offset the interest
About $540/year (full interest saving, ignoring lost rewards)
About $360/year (just the lost rewards, ignoring interest saving)
correctConceptChoice: About $180/year (interest saved by switching to a 15% APR card exceeds the lost rewards)

promptTemplate: When does a cashback / points credit card actually pay for itself in real dollars?
explanationTemplate: Only when you pay the statement balance in full every month. Cashback at 2% sounds great but is mathematically destroyed by a 22% APR the moment you carry any balance. The 'rewards card vs low-APR card' decision is the second most important credit-card decision after 'pay in full every month.' Anyone carrying a balance should switch to the lowest-APR card they qualify for, accept lower rewards (or none), and prioritize debt payoff.
conceptChoices: Only when you pay the statement balance in full every month
Always — 2% back is 2% back
Only on holiday months when spend is concentrated
Only on cards with annual fees
correctConceptChoice: Only when you pay the statement balance in full every month

promptTemplate: You want to save ${{expense}} for a known irregular expense {{monthsAway}} months from now. How much should the sinking fund contribute each month?
explanationTemplate: Monthly = expense ÷ months until needed = ${{expense}} ÷ {{monthsAway}} = ${{answer}}/month. Round up for safety. The point: a single monthly line replaces a single big-month shock that breaks the budget. Multiple sinking funds for different expenses run simultaneously — total monthly outlay typically lands $200-500 for 4-6 funds combined.

promptTemplate: You're running four sinking funds: Holiday ${{holiday}}/mo, Travel ${{travel}}/mo, Car Maintenance ${{car}}/mo, Gifts ${{gifts}}/mo. What's your total monthly sinking-fund outlay?
explanationTemplate: Total = sum of all funds = ${{holiday}} + ${{travel}} + ${{car}} + ${{gifts}} = ${{answer}}/month. Treat this as part of the 'needs' bucket in the 50/30/20 rule (predictable, just irregular timing) — not 'wants.' Misclassifying sinking funds as discretionary is the #1 reason monthly budgets feel structurally broken every couple of months.

promptTemplate: Today is {{startMonth}}. You want to have ${{holidayBudget}} for holiday spending (gifts + travel + extras) by the end of November. How much per month do you need to put aside?
explanationTemplate: Months until November = 12 − start month + 1. Monthly = ${{holidayBudget}} ÷ (12 − {{startMonth}} + 1) = ${{answer}}. Holiday spending is the canonical sinking-fund use case — it's predictable, large, and hits every year. Starting in January gives you 11 months to spread; starting in October leaves only 2 months and forces credit-card use that costs interest.

promptTemplate: You found out 2 months ago about a wedding 5 months from now. Estimated total cost (gift + travel + outfit): ${{weddingCost}}. You've saved nothing yet. Monthly sinking fund needed for the next 5 months?
explanationTemplate: Monthly = ${{weddingCost}} ÷ 5 = ${{answer}}. Short windows hurt — the same cost over 12 months would be less than half the monthly hit. The takeaway: as soon as you know about ANY irregular expense (>2 months out), start the sinking fund immediately. Even partial funding over a long window beats a full-on credit-card hit the week before.

promptTemplate: Why use a sinking fund instead of just charging the irregular expense to a credit card and paying it off over a few months?
explanationTemplate: A $1,500 holiday expense paid down over 3 months on a 22% APR credit card costs ~$50 in interest. The sinking-fund alternative ($125/mo for 12 months) costs $0 in interest AND earns ~4-5% APY in a HYSA (~$30 of free interest). Net difference: $80 saved + behavior locked in for next year (recurring fund replenishes automatically). Charging the credit card creates a recurring 'oh that hurt' moment that nudges the next irregular expense onto the credit card too — sinking funds break that cycle.
conceptChoices: Avoid the 22%+ APR interest on the credit-card balance
Credit cards don't allow large purchases
Sinking funds get a tax deduction
Credit cards damage your credit even when paid off
correctConceptChoice: Avoid the 22%+ APR interest on the credit-card balance

promptTemplate: Using the mental anchor ($100/mo at 8% × 30 yrs ≈ $150K), roughly how much per month do you need to invest to reach ${{goal}} in 30 years at 8% nominal return?
explanationTemplate: Monthly ≈ goal × $100 ÷ $150K = goal × 0.000667. For ${{goal}}: ${{answer}}/month. Mental check: $1M ÷ $150K × $100 = ~$667/mo. The exact annuity-formula answer is within 3-5% of this scaling — close enough for goal-setting. Adjust if your time horizon is different (use the anchor table in the lesson: 20yr → $59K, 25yr → $95K, 35yr → $230K, 40yr → $330K per $100/mo).

promptTemplate: Target $1,000,000 by retirement at 8% nominal return. How much per month if you start with {{years}} years to go?
explanationTemplate: At 8% annual: monthly = $1M × (r/12) ÷ ((1 + r/12)^(years × 12) − 1). For {{years}} years: ${{answer}}/month. Big picture: 40 years = ~$300/mo, 30 years = ~$670/mo, 20 years = ~$1,700/mo. Every 10 years earlier roughly cuts the monthly contribution in half. Time is more powerful than amount for long horizons.

promptTemplate: Target $500,000 in 25 years at 8% nominal return. Using the anchor ($100/mo × 25 yrs at 8% ≈ $95K), roughly how much per month?
explanationTemplate: $500K ÷ $95K × $100 ≈ $530/mo. The exact annuity-formula answer is ~$525/mo — within 1% of the mental shortcut. The anchor table works well for any goal-horizon combination: just scale linearly from the appropriate row.
conceptChoices: About $525/month
About $200/month
About $1,000/month
About $1,667/month (just $500K ÷ 25 yrs ÷ 12, ignoring growth)
correctConceptChoice: About $525/month

promptTemplate: Target $2,000,000 in 35 years at 8% nominal return. Using the anchor ($100/mo × 35 yrs ≈ $230K), about how much per month?
explanationTemplate: $2M ÷ $230K × $100 ≈ $870/mo. Exact annuity: ~$870/mo. The anchor scales beautifully for higher targets too. The 35-year horizon makes $2M much more accessible — at 20 years, you'd need ~$3,400/mo, nearly 4× higher.
conceptChoices: About $870/month
About $400/month
About $2,500/month
About $4,800/month
correctConceptChoice: About $870/month

promptTemplate: To hit $1M at 8% nominal return, Ava starts at 25 ($300/mo × 40 yrs) and Kenji starts at 45 ($1,700/mo × 20 yrs). Both end at $1M. Who contributes LESS total dollars over the horizon?
explanationTemplate: Ava: $300/mo × 12 × 40 = $144,000 total contributed. Kenji: $1,700/mo × 12 × 20 = $408,000 total contributed. Ava contributes $264K LESS in absolute dollars to reach the same $1M — because 20 extra years of compounding does the heavy lifting. This is the math behind 'start early' — it's not just a slogan, the early starter's total cash outlay is dramatically lower.
conceptChoices: Ava — $144K total contributions vs Kenji's $408K, despite hitting the same $1M
Kenji — higher monthly means lower total since the horizon is shorter
They contribute exactly the same — the math works out evenly
Impossible to compare without knowing tax bracket
correctConceptChoice: Ava — $144K total contributions vs Kenji's $408K, despite hitting the same $1M

promptTemplate: You receive a ${{bonus}} year-end bonus. You're in TX (no state income tax). 22% federal supplemental withholding (per IRS Pub 15) + 7.65% FICA. What's your bonus take-home?
explanationTemplate: Take-home = bonus × (1 − 22% − 7.65%) = bonus × 0.7035 = ${{answer}}. In a no-state-tax state, only federal supplemental + FICA apply. Note: 22% is WITHHOLDING (per IRS Pub 15), not the final tax. If your marginal federal bracket is higher than 22%, expect to owe more at filing.

promptTemplate: You receive a ${{bonus}} year-end bonus in {{stateRate}}% state (combined state + local effective rate). 22% federal supplemental + 7.65% FICA + state. What's your take-home?
explanationTemplate: Take-home = bonus × (1 − 22% − 7.65% − stateRate%) = ${{answer}}. On $10K bonus in CA (9.3% effective): ~$6,105 take-home. On the same bonus in NYC (combined ~10% NY state + city): ~$6,035. State tax + city tax compound quickly on bonuses.

promptTemplate: You're in the {{marginalBracket}}% federal marginal bracket. You get a ${{bonus}} bonus. 22% federal supplemental was withheld. How much MORE federal tax do you owe at filing on this bonus?
explanationTemplate: Extra owed = bonus × (marginal − 22%) = ${{bonus}} × ({{marginalBracket}}% − 22%) = ${{answer}}. The 22% supplemental rate is one-size-fits-all (per IRS Pub 15). For workers in 24%+ brackets, the withholding under-collects. Set aside this gap in a HYSA when the bonus hits — don't spend the take-home as if it's final.

promptTemplate: You're in the 12% federal marginal bracket. You get a $5,000 bonus. 22% federal supplemental was withheld. How much OVER-withholding will be refunded at filing time (just the federal portion)?
explanationTemplate: Over-withholding = bonus × (22% − marginal%) = $5,000 × (22% − 12%) = $500 federal refunded at filing. For lower-bracket earners, the 22% supplemental rate over-collects — this is effectively a forced savings that gets returned with the refund. Note: state withholding may also be over- or under-collected separately.
conceptChoices: $0 — withholding always matches

promptTemplate: True or false: the 22% federal supplemental withholding rate on bonuses is your actual federal tax rate on that money.
explanationTemplate: FALSE. 22% is the WITHHOLDING rate (per IRS Pub 15) — what your employer holds back when issuing the bonus. Your ACTUAL federal tax is determined at filing by your marginal bracket. If you're in the 32% bracket, the bonus is ultimately taxed at 32% — you'll owe the extra 10% at filing. If you're in the 12% bracket, you'll get the over-withholding refunded. The 22% is a placeholder rate, not the final answer.
conceptChoices: False — 22% is just withholding; actual tax is determined by your marginal bracket at filing
True — 22% is the flat tax rate for bonuses
True — but only if you make under $1M in supplemental wages
False — bonuses aren't subject to federal income tax
correctConceptChoice: False — 22% is just withholding; actual tax is determined by your marginal bracket at filing

scenarioTemplate: You earn $60,000/yr ($5,000/mo gross). A $30,000 car is offered with $2,000 down, a 7-year loan at about $430/mo; insurance + gas run about $250/mo.
promptTemplate: Does this fit the 20/4/10 guideline, and what should you do?
explanationTemplate: The 20/4/10 rule: put 20% down ($6,000, not $2,000), finance no more than 4 years (not 7), and keep ALL car costs under 10% of gross income ($500/mo; you're at ~$680 with the payment plus insurance and gas). This deal misses all three, signaling real risk of being stretched and underwater. The fix is a cheaper car, a bigger down payment, or a shorter term — not a longer loan.
conceptChoices: No — it misses on all three: too little down, too long a term, and ~$680/mo of car costs against a $500 budget. Look at a cheaper car or save a bigger down payment
Yes — $430/mo is well under $500, so it's affordable
No, but only because the down payment is low; the term and the budget are fine
Yes — 7-year car loans are normal now, so the rule no longer applies
correctConceptChoice: No — it misses on all three: too little down, too long a term, and ~$680/mo of car costs against a $500 budget. Look at a cheaper car or save a bigger down payment

scenarioTemplate: Same $25,000 car, two financing offers. Option A: 48 months at $575/mo. Option B: 72 months at $410/mo — the salesperson says it's '$165 a month cheaper.'
promptTemplate: Which is the better deal, and why?
explanationTemplate: Total cost = monthly payment × number of months. Option A: $575 × 48 = $27,600. Option B: $410 × 72 = $29,520. The longer term's lower payment actually costs about $1,920 MORE in total and keeps you owing more than the car is worth (underwater) for far longer. Always compare total cost, not the monthly payment — a smaller payment from a longer loan is usually more expensive.
conceptChoices: The 48-month loan — the 72-month's lower payment actually costs about $1,920 more in total ($29,520 vs $27,600) and keeps you underwater longer
The 72-month loan — a lower monthly payment is always the cheaper choice
They cost the same; you're just spreading the payments differently
The 72-month loan — paying for longer builds more credit history
correctConceptChoice: The 48-month loan — the 72-month's lower payment actually costs about $1,920 more in total ($29,520 vs $27,600) and keeps you underwater longer

scenarioTemplate: You typically keep a car 8+ years. Lease: $350/mo, and you re-lease again every 3 years. Buy: $480/mo for 5 years, then $0 for years 6-8 once it's paid off.
promptTemplate: For someone who keeps cars 8+ years, which is usually cheaper?
explanationTemplate: Over 8 years: buying costs $480 × 60 = $28,800, then $0 for the last 36 months — and you own the car. Leasing costs $350 × 96 = $33,600 with nothing to show for it. Leasing's lower monthly payment is tempting, but you never stop paying and never build an asset. Leasing tends to win only if you want a new car every 2-3 years and value low payments over ownership.
conceptChoices: Buying — you pay $480/mo for 5 years then nothing for years 6-8 and own the car; leasing means paying $350/mo forever and never owning
Leasing — the lower $350/mo payment makes it cheaper every month
Leasing — you always get a newer car, so it's automatically the better value
They cost about the same over 8 years
correctConceptChoice: Buying — you pay $480/mo for 5 years then nothing for years 6-8 and own the car; leasing means paying $350/mo forever and never owning

scenarioTemplate: You have $40,000 in federal student loans at 6.5%. A private lender offers to refinance to 5.0%, saving about $30/mo. You work at a nonprofit and may pursue public-service loan forgiveness (PSLF).
promptTemplate: Should you take the refinance, and why?
explanationTemplate: Refinancing federal loans into a private loan is a one-way door: you permanently give up PSLF, income-driven repayment, and federal forbearance/deferment. If you might pursue public-service forgiveness, that could mean your whole balance forgiven — worth far more than the ~$30/mo a small rate cut saves. Refinancing mainly makes sense for high-rate PRIVATE loans, or federal loans you're certain you'll repay in full and won't need the safety nets for.
conceptChoices: No — refinancing federal loans into a private loan is permanent and forfeits PSLF and income-driven repayment, which are worth far more than $30/mo on a forgiveness track
Yes — a lower interest rate always saves money, so refinance
Yes — the $30/mo savings compounds to a large amount over 10 years
No — but only because a 1.5-point rate drop isn't big enough
correctConceptChoice: No — refinancing federal loans into a private loan is permanent and forfeits PSLF and income-driven repayment, which are worth far more than $30/mo on a forgiveness track

scenarioTemplate: You graduate with $30,000 in UNSUBSIDIZED federal loans at 6%. During your 6-month grace period, interest accrues at about $150/mo. You can pay the ~$900 of grace-period interest now, or let it capitalize (be added to your principal).
promptTemplate: What's the smarter move?
explanationTemplate: Unsubsidized loans accrue interest even during school and the grace period. If you don't pay it, that interest CAPITALIZES — it's added to your principal when repayment starts, so you then pay interest on a bigger balance (interest on interest). Paying the ~$900 during grace keeps your principal at $30,000. (Subsidized loans are different: the government covers the interest during school and grace, so this doesn't apply to them.)
conceptChoices: Pay the ~$900 of interest before it capitalizes — otherwise it's added to your $30,000 principal and you pay interest on it for years
Let it capitalize — interest during the grace period is free
Let it capitalize — $900 is too small to matter
Pay it only if your loans are subsidized
correctConceptChoice: Pay the ~$900 of interest before it capitalizes — otherwise it's added to your $30,000 principal and you pay interest on it for years

scenarioTemplate: You'll graduate owing about $50,000 in federal loans (~6% over 10 years ≈ $555/mo). Your field's typical starting salary is about $45,000/yr (~$3,000/mo take-home).
promptTemplate: Is this a manageable debt load, and what does it imply?
explanationTemplate: A common guideline: keep total student-loan payments under ~10% of gross income, and try to keep total borrowing at or below your expected first-year salary. Here, $50,000 of debt ≈ your $45,000 salary (borderline), and $555/mo is roughly 18% of your take-home — about double the comfortable level. It doesn't mean don't go, but it's a signal to borrow less where you can and plan for a lean first year or two.
conceptChoices: It's on the high side — $555/mo is about 18% of your take-home, well above the ~10% guideline. Consider borrowing less or planning for a tight budget early on
It's fine — $555/mo is affordable on any salary
It's hopeless — you'll never be able to repay $50,000
It's fine because federal loans are always affordable no matter the balance
correctConceptChoice: It's on the high side — $555/mo is about 18% of your take-home, well above the ~10% guideline. Consider borrowing less or planning for a tight budget early on

scenarioTemplate: You owe $6,000 on a card at 24% APR. A balance-transfer offer gives you 0% APR for 15 months with a 3% transfer fee, and you can pay about $420/mo.
promptTemplate: Is the balance transfer worth it, and what's the catch?
explanationTemplate: A balance transfer trades a one-time fee for a 0% window. The fee is 3% × $6,000 = $180. At 24% APR, paying $6,000 down over ~15 months costs roughly $900+ in interest, so the transfer saves you several hundred dollars. It only works if you clear the balance before the 0% promo ends — here $420/mo × 15 = $6,300 covers the $6,180 owed. If you don't pay it off in time, the rate jumps back up. Don't add new charges to either card.
conceptChoices: Yes — the $180 fee (3% of $6,000) is far less than the ~$900+ of interest at 24%, and $420/mo clears it within the 0% window. The catch: pay it off before the promo ends
No — a 3% fee means you're just paying to shuffle debt around
Yes — and you can take your time since it's 0% interest
No — balance transfers always damage your credit score too much
correctConceptChoice: Yes — the $180 fee (3% of $6,000) is far less than the ~$900+ of interest at 24%, and $420/mo clears it within the 0% window. The catch: pay it off before the promo ends

scenarioTemplate: Your card gives 2% cash back. You're carrying a $3,000 balance at 22% APR and paying the minimum. You're tempted to put more spending on the card to rack up rewards.
promptTemplate: Should you chase the rewards, and why?
explanationTemplate: Card rewards (typically 1-2%) only come out ahead if you pay the balance in full every month. Carrying $3,000 at 22% costs about $660/yr in interest — you'd have to spend $33,000 to earn that much back at 2%. While you carry a balance, every reward is swamped by interest. The move: stop adding charges, pay down the balance, then use the card for rewards once you can clear it in full each month.
conceptChoices: No — 2% back is meaningless next to 22% interest on your $3,000 balance (~$660/yr). Stop new charges and pay it down; rewards only pay off when you clear the card monthly
Yes — free cash back is free money, always take it
Yes — as long as the rewards rate beats your minimum payment
No — but only because 2% is a low rewards rate
correctConceptChoice: No — 2% back is meaningless next to 22% interest on your $3,000 balance (~$660/yr). Stop new charges and pay it down; rewards only pay off when you clear the card monthly

scenarioTemplate: You have $0 saved and $5,000 in credit card debt at 23% APR. You can put $300/mo toward either a starter emergency fund or the card.
promptTemplate: What's the recommended order, and why?
explanationTemplate: Build a tiny starter emergency fund (around $1,000) first — without it, the next surprise (car repair, medical bill) goes straight back onto the 23% card and undoes your progress. Once you have that cushion, attack the high-interest debt aggressively: paying off 23% debt is a guaranteed 23% 'return' you can't beat by saving. Build the full 3-6 month fund AFTER the high-interest debt is gone. Order: starter fund → high-interest debt → full fund.
conceptChoices: Build a small ~$1,000 starter emergency fund first, then throw everything at the 23% card — the cushion keeps a surprise from forcing you back onto the card
Put every dollar on the card first; an emergency fund can wait until you're debt-free
Split it 50/50 between the fund and the card indefinitely
Build a full 6-month emergency fund before paying anything extra on the card
correctConceptChoice: Build a small ~$1,000 starter emergency fund first, then throw everything at the 23% card — the cushion keeps a surprise from forcing you back onto the card

scenarioTemplate: A warehouse-store membership costs $65/yr. You estimate you save about $4 per visit versus regular stores, and you shop there about twice a month.
promptTemplate: Is the membership worth it, and what's the catch?
explanationTemplate: A membership pays off when annual savings beat the fee AND it doesn't drive extra spending. Here: 24 visits × $4 = $96 saved vs a $65 fee → net +$31. The trap is the 'I have the membership, might as well buy more' impulse — bulk buys you didn't need can erase the savings. Worth it if your real usage clears the fee and your spending stays disciplined.
conceptChoices: Worth it — about $96/yr in savings (24 visits × $4) beats the $65 fee, as long as it doesn't push you into impulse buys
Not worth it — any membership fee is just money down the drain
Worth it — memberships always save more the more you spend
Not worth it — $4 a visit is too small to ever add up
correctConceptChoice: Worth it — about $96/yr in savings (24 visits × $4) beats the $65 fee, as long as it doesn't push you into impulse buys

scenarioTemplate: A $200 jacket. Store A: 25% off. Store B: a $40-off coupon. Sales tax is 8% at both.
promptTemplate: Which store gives you the better price?
explanationTemplate: Convert the percent to dollars: 25% of $200 = $50 off, which beats the $40 flat coupon. After 8% tax, Store A is $150 × 1.08 = $162 vs Store B's $160 × 1.08 = $172.80 — a $10.80 difference. Tax hits both, so it doesn't change which is cheaper; compare the discounts in dollars.
conceptChoices: Store A — 25% off $200 is $50 off (final $162 after tax), beating the $40 coupon (final $172.80)
Store B — a flat $40 coupon is a guaranteed discount
They come out the same once tax is added
Store B — percentages always sound bigger than they really are
correctConceptChoice: Store A — 25% off $200 is $50 off (final $162 after tax), beating the $40 coupon (final $172.80)

scenarioTemplate: A $100 coat. The sign says '30% off, then an extra 20% off at checkout.' You're expecting to pay $50 (a 50% discount).
promptTemplate: What will you actually pay, and why isn't it $50?
explanationTemplate: Stacked discounts apply one after another, so they multiply rather than add. $100 × 0.70 = $70, then × 0.80 = $56 — a 44% total cut, not 50%. The second discount comes off the already-reduced price, so '30% then 20%' always falls short of a flat 50%.
conceptChoices: $56 — the discounts multiply ($100 → $70 → $56), a 44% total cut, not the 50% you'd get by adding 30% + 20%
$56 — but only because of sales tax
$44 — you subtract both discounts straight from $100
correctConceptChoice: $56 — the discounts multiply ($100 → $70 → $56), a 44% total cut, not the 50% you'd get by adding 30% + 20%

scenarioTemplate: You take home $4,000/mo. Your needs (rent, utilities, groceries, minimum debt payments) run $2,600. Under 50/30/20, needs should be about $2,000.
promptTemplate: Is this budget on track, and what does it mean?
explanationTemplate: 50/30/20 splits take-home into 50% needs / 30% wants / 20% savings. Here needs are $2,600 = 65% of $4,000 — well over the 50% ($2,000) target, leaving only 35% for wants AND savings combined. The usual lever is the biggest fixed cost, housing (a roommate or cheaper place), or raising income. The ratios are a guideline, but 65% on needs is a real warning sign.

scenarioTemplate: Your essential monthly expenses are $3,000. You're a single renter with a stable salaried job, and you have $2,000 saved.
promptTemplate: What's a reasonable emergency-fund target, and where do you stand?
explanationTemplate: A common emergency-fund target is 3-6 months of ESSENTIAL expenses ($9,000-$18,000 here). With a single, stable salaried income, the lower end (~3 months, $9,000) is a reasonable floor; volatile or single-earner-with-dependents situations lean higher. At $2,000 you have under a month — keep building the cushion in a high-yield savings account before putting extra into investments.
conceptChoices: About $9,000 (3 months of essentials) is a reasonable floor for a stable single income; at $2,000 you're well short, so keep building the fund

Skip the fund and invest instead — markets return more than savings
correctConceptChoice: About $9,000 (3 months of essentials) is a reasonable floor for a stable single income; at $2,000 you're well short, so keep building the fund

scenarioTemplate: It's January. You know you'll spend about $1,200 on holiday gifts in December and $600 on car registration in March.
promptTemplate: What's the smart way to handle these known irregular costs?
explanationTemplate: Sinking funds turn lumpy, predictable expenses into smooth monthly savings. Divide each cost by the months until it's due: $1,200 ÷ 11 ≈ $109/mo for December gifts, $600 ÷ 2 = $300/mo for March registration. When the bill arrives, the money's already there — no scramble, no credit-card interest. This is how you budget for 'surprises' that aren't actually surprises.
conceptChoices: Start sinking funds now — save ~$109/mo for December gifts ($1,200÷11) and ~$300/mo for March registration ($600÷2) so neither is a shock
Wait until the bills arrive and put them on a credit card
Ignore them — they're too far away to plan for
Save the full $1,800 this month to be safe
correctConceptChoice: Start sinking funds now — save ~$109/mo for December gifts ($1,200÷11) and ~$300/mo for March registration ($600÷2) so neither is a shock

scenarioTemplate: You earn $60,000. Your employer matches 100% of your 401(k) contributions up to 5% of pay. You currently contribute 2%.
promptTemplate: What should you do, and why?
explanationTemplate: An employer match is free money — here, 100% up to 5% of pay. 5% of $60,000 = $3,000 of match available; at 2% ($1,200) you only capture $1,200, leaving about $1,800/yr unclaimed. Contributing enough to get the full match is the highest-return move in personal finance — an instant 100% return before any market growth. Hit at least the match, even if you can't contribute more.
conceptChoices: Raise your contribution to at least 5% — you're leaving about $1,800/yr of free employer match on the table, and the match is an instant 100% return
Stay at 2% — any 401(k) contribution is good enough
Stop contributing — you can't touch the money until retirement
Go to 5% only if you can also max the full annual limit
correctConceptChoice: Raise your contribution to at least 5% — you're leaving about $1,800/yr of free employer match on the table, and the match is an instant 100% return

scenarioTemplate: Two offers for the same work: a W-2 job at $45/hr, or a 1099 contract at $50/hr. The 1099 has no benefits — you cover both halves of payroll tax (~7.65% extra) plus your own health insurance.
promptTemplate: Is the $50/hr 1099 actually the better deal?
explanationTemplate: A 1099 contractor pays BOTH halves of Social Security/Medicare (~15.3% total vs ~7.65% for an employee), so about 7.65% comes off the top. You also lose employer health insurance (often $400-600/mo of value), PTO, and any 401(k) match. A common rule of thumb: a 1099 rate should be ~25-30% higher than a W-2 rate to break even. At only 11% more ($50 vs $45), the W-2 is often the better deal once benefits are counted.
conceptChoices: Not necessarily — the extra ~7.65% self-employment tax plus lost health insurance, PTO, and 401(k) match often make the 1099 worth LESS than the $45 W-2; a rule of thumb is it should pay ~25-30% more to break even
Yes — $50 is more than $45, so always take the 1099

correctConceptChoice: Not necessarily — the extra ~7.65% self-employment tax plus lost health insurance, PTO, and 401(k) match often make the 1099 worth LESS than the $45 W-2; a rule of thumb is it should pay ~25-30% more to break even

scenarioTemplate: Two job offers for similar work: a $50,000 salary, or $26/hr at 40 hours/week.
promptTemplate: Which offer pays more, and what else matters?
explanationTemplate: Convert to the same basis: a full-time year is about 2,080 hours (40 hrs × 52 weeks). $26 × 2,080 = $54,080, which beats the $50,000 salary by about $4,080. Hourly (non-exempt) roles are also overtime-eligible (1.5× past 40 hrs/week), while salaried (exempt) roles usually aren't. Always convert offers to the same time basis before comparing — and weigh benefits and overtime too.

$26/hr — but only if you work more than 40 hours a week

scenarioTemplate: Two similar funds. Fund A: 1.0% expense ratio. Fund B: a 0.05% index fund. You invest $10,000/yr for 30 years at about a 7% return before fees.
promptTemplate: Which fund should you pick, and how much does the fee really matter?
explanationTemplate: Fees compound against you. Investing $10,000/yr for 30 years: at ~7% net (Fund B) you'd have roughly $944,000; at ~6% net (Fund A's extra ~1% fee) roughly $791,000 — about $150,000 less, for funds that may perform identically before fees. Higher fees do NOT predict better returns. Minimizing expense ratios is one of the few levers fully in your control.

Fund A — a 1% fee is tiny and not worth worrying about
Whichever one performed better over the last year
Fund A — higher fees signal better fund management
correctConceptChoice: Fund B (0.05%) — a ~1% higher fee quietly compounds to roughly $150,000 less over 30 years; low fees are one of the few things you control

scenarioTemplate: You're early in your career in a low tax bracket (12%) and expect to earn much more later. You're choosing between a Roth and a Traditional IRA.
promptTemplate: Which generally makes more sense, and why?
explanationTemplate: The Roth-vs-Traditional choice hinges on your tax rate NOW vs in retirement. Roth = pay tax now, withdraw tax-free. Traditional = deduct now, pay tax on withdrawals. In a low bracket today (12%) and expecting more later, a Roth wins: you lock in the cheap 12% rate and never pay tax on the growth. If you expect a LOWER rate in retirement, Traditional's upfront deduction wins. When genuinely unsure, many people split between the two.
conceptChoices: Roth — in a low bracket now and a higher one expected later, paying 12% tax now and withdrawing tax-free beats deducting at 12% and being taxed more later
Traditional — the upfront deduction is always the better deal
It never matters; the two are identical
Roth — but only if you'll retire before age 50
correctConceptChoice: Roth — in a low bracket now and a higher one expected later, paying 12% tax now and withdrawing tax-free beats deducting at 12% and being taxed more later

scenarioTemplate: Ana invests $5,000/yr from age 25-35 (10 years, $50k total), then stops and never adds more. Ben invests $5,000/yr from age 35-65 (30 years, $150k total). Both earn about 7%.
promptTemplate: Who has more at 65, and what's the lesson?
explanationTemplate: This is the power of compounding. Ana invests $5,000/yr for just 10 years (ages 25-35, $50k total), then lets it grow untouched. Ben invests $5,000/yr for 30 years (ages 35-65, $150k total). At ~7%, Ana ends with roughly $526,000 vs Ben's ~$472,000 — more, despite investing a third as much, because her money compounded for an extra decade. Starting early matters more than investing more later.
conceptChoices: Ana — despite investing only $50k vs Ben's $150k, her early start gives the money decades more to compound (~$526k vs ~$472k). Time in the market beats amount
Ben — he invested three times as much, so he must have more
They end up equal — it all comes out the same
Ana — but only because she got lucky with returns
correctConceptChoice: Ana — despite investing only $50k vs Ben's $150k, her early start gives the money decades more to compound (~$526k vs ~$472k). Time in the market beats amount

scenarioTemplate: You earn $4,500/mo gross. An apartment you love rents for $1,600/mo. The 28% rule says housing should be at most about 28% of gross.

explanationTemplate: The 28% rule suggests keeping housing at or below 28% of gross — here, $1,260/mo. scenarioTemplate: You're comparing renting at $1,800/mo to buying with a $1,800/mo mortgage payment (principal + interest). The agent says, 'It's the same price to own as to rent!'
promptTemplate: Is owning really the 'same price' as renting here?
explanationTemplate: A mortgage payment quoted as '$1,800' is usually just principal and interest. Real ownership cost adds property taxes, homeowners insurance, maintenance (budget ~1% of the home's value per year), and possibly HOA or PMI — often another $400-800/mo. scenarioTemplate: You have 5 months left on a $1,500/mo lease. A new job across town would cut ~90 min/day of commuting, and the apartment near it is $200/mo cheaper. Breaking your current lease costs a 2-month penalty ($3,000).
promptTemplate: How should you decide?
explanationTemplate: A lease-break decision is cost vs total benefit. Cost: the $3,000 penalty (plus any lost deposit). Benefit: cheaper rent ($200/mo), ~90 min/day of your life back, lower commute costs, and the new job's value. Add up the real benefit and weigh it against $3,000 — don't fixate on one factor. (Breaking a lease per its terms doesn't directly hurt your credit; only an unpaid balance sent to collections does.)

Always stay — breaking a lease wrecks your credit score
Always break it — a shorter commute is worth any price
Only break it if the penalty is under one month's rent
correctConceptChoice: Weigh the $3,000 penalty against the FULL benefit — rent savings, ~90 min/day back, and the job itself — not just one piece. If the total beats $3,000, break it

scenarioTemplate: You get a $3,600 tax refund every year and feel great about it. That's about $300/mo.
promptTemplate: What does this refund really mean, and what could you do?
explanationTemplate: A tax refund isn't a gift — it's your own money coming back because too much was withheld all year. A $3,600 refund is roughly $300/mo you lent the government interest-free. Adjusting your W-4 to withhold less puts that ~$300/mo back in each paycheck, where you can spend, save, or invest it sooner. (Some people like the refund as forced savings — a real behavioral trade-off, but you give up use of the money in the meantime.)

Refunds are free money the government adds to your taxes

scenarioTemplate: You earn $48,000 and get a raise to $52,000. A coworker warns: 'Careful — that bump pushes you into the next tax bracket, so you might actually take home less!'
promptTemplate: Is the coworker right?
explanationTemplate: US federal income tax is MARGINAL: each bracket's rate applies only to the income within that bracket, not your whole income. Going from $48,000 to $52,000 means only the income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate — the rest is unchanged. So a raise always increases your take-home. (The rare exception is a benefit 'cliff' — losing a subsidy at an income limit — which is about benefits, not tax brackets.)

scenarioTemplate: You bought a stock 11 months ago; it's up $5,000. You're in the 22% bracket. Sell now and the gain is short-term (taxed as ordinary income, 22%); wait one more month and it's long-term (taxed at the 15% long-term rate).
promptTemplate: What's the tax-smart move, and the caveat?
explanationTemplate: Gains on assets held ONE YEAR OR LESS are short-term, taxed as ordinary income (22% here). Held MORE than a year, they're long-term, taxed at preferential rates (0/15/20%; 15% for most middle incomes). On a $5,000 gain that's $1,100 (short-term) vs $750 (long-term) — waiting one more month saves $350 if the price holds. The caveat: don't let the 'tax tail wag the dog' — if you'd sell for investment reasons, a price drop can cost more than the tax saved.

scenarioTemplate: You owe $4,000 on a card at 24% APR. The minimum payment is about $100/mo (mostly interest). You could instead pay a fixed $250/mo.
promptTemplate: What's the smart move, and why is the minimum a trap?
explanationTemplate: The 'minimum payment trap': minimums are set low (often ~2-3% of the balance), and at 24% APR most of that goes to interest, so the balance barely moves. Paying a FIXED amount above the minimum — here $250/mo — clears the $4,000 in about 19 months. Paying only the declining minimum can stretch the same debt across many years and roughly double its cost. The fix: pick a fixed payment you can sustain and hold it steady.

Pay the minimum — it's the responsible, on-time choice

correctConceptChoice: Pay a fixed $250/mo — that clears the $4,000 in about 19 months. Paying only the ~$100 minimum keeps you in debt for years because most of it goes to interest, not principal

scenarioTemplate: You found a house you can afford, but you might relocate for work in about 2 years. Buying and later selling carries roughly 6-9%+ in transaction costs (closing fees to buy, agent commission to sell).
promptTemplate: Given a likely move in ~2 years, what generally makes more sense?
explanationTemplate: The biggest factor in buy-vs-rent is your TIME HORIZON. Buying then selling carries large one-time costs — roughly 2-5% to buy plus ~6% agent commission to sell, often 8-11% round-trip — and it usually takes several years of equity and appreciation just to break even on them. With a likely move in ~2 years, renting typically wins; buying tends to pay off only when you'll stay ~5+ years. 'Throwing money away on rent' ignores the interest, taxes, and maintenance you also can't recover as an owner.

correctConceptChoice: Renting — buying and selling carries ~6-9%+ in transaction costs that rarely recoup in just 2 years; buying usually wins only with a longer horizon (~5+ years)

scenarioTemplate: You earn $5,000/mo gross. Your current debt payments (car + student loan + card minimums) total $1,400/mo. You're applying for a mortgage; lenders usually cap total debt-to-income — including the new housing payment — near 43%.
promptTemplate: What does your DTI mean for the mortgage?
explanationTemplate: Debt-to-income (DTI) = monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income. Lenders look at TOTAL DTI including the new housing payment, usually capping near 43%. Here, $5,000 × 43% = $2,150; minus your existing $1,400 leaves only ~$750/mo for the mortgage + taxes + insurance. Paying down existing debt (especially the card and car) frees up room to qualify for more.

correctConceptChoice: Your $1,400 of payments is 28% of income; with the ~43% total cap ($2,150), only ~$750/mo is left for housing. Pay down debt first to qualify for more

scenarioTemplate: You have three debts: $2,000 at 24%, $5,000 at 7%, and $800 at 19%. You have $300/mo extra to throw at one. A friend says 'pay the smallest first for momentum.'
promptTemplate: Which order saves you the most money?
explanationTemplate: Two methods: AVALANCHE pays the highest interest rate first (here the 24% card, then 19%, then 7%), minimizing total interest — the cheapest path. SNOWBALL pays the smallest balance first ($800) for quick psychological wins, which can help you stick with it but costs more interest. The math favors avalanche; if motivation has been your problem, snowball's momentum can be worth the small extra cost. Either beats spreading the $300 thin.

correctConceptChoice: Avalanche — put the extra $300 on the 24% debt first, then 19%, then 7%. That minimizes total interest. Snowball (smallest first) helps motivation but costs more

scenarioTemplate: A $600 item is offered as 'Pay in 4 — $150 every 2 weeks, 0% interest.' You have the $600 in the bank.

Rule: only use it for something you could pay for in full today, and never to stretch for something you can't.
conceptChoices: If you have the cash and pay on time, 0% 'pay in 4' is fine — but it nudges you to buy more than you would with cash, and a missed payment means fees. Don't use it for things you couldn't afford outright

scenarioTemplate: You just got a $12,000 windfall to invest for retirement (30 years out). You're nervous about putting it all in at once in case the market drops next month.
promptTemplate: What's the reasonable approach?
explanationTemplate: With a 30-year horizon, the biggest risk isn't a bad month — it's staying in cash and missing decades of growth. Historically, investing a lump sum immediately beats dollar-cost-averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets rise more often than they fall. But DCA (spreading it over, say, 3-6 months) is a reasonable compromise if a sudden drop would make you panic-sell. Either is far better than waiting for a 'safe' moment that never feels safe.
conceptChoices: Get invested — over 30 years, time IN the market beats timing it. Lump sum usually wins historically; if a drop would rattle you, spread it over a few months. Just don't sit in cash waiting
Wait in cash until the market 'feels safe'

At $30,000 vs a $60,000 salary you're at ~0.5× — behind, but not alarmingly so at 30, when decades of compounding do the heavy lifting. Right on track — $30,000 is plenty at 30

scenarioTemplate: You keep $10,000 of savings in a checking account earning 0.01% APY. A high-yield savings account (HYSA) offers about 4% APY, FDIC-insured.
promptTemplate: Should you move the money, and what's the catch?
explanationTemplate: A high-yield savings account is just a savings account that pays a competitive rate (often ~4% lately) instead of near-zero. scenarioTemplate: Your rent is going from $1,500 to $1,650 (+10%) at renewal. A comparable place across town is $1,500/mo, but moving costs about $2,500 (deposit, movers, fees) plus your time.
promptTemplate: Renew or move — and what should you try first?
explanationTemplate: Compare the ongoing savings to the one-time cost. Moving to the $1,500 place saves $150/mo vs the $1,650 renewal, but moving costs ~$2,500 — so the break-even is about $2,500 ÷ $150 ≈ 17 months. If you'll stay longer, moving wins; if not, renewing is cheaper once you count moving costs and hassle. Before deciding, negotiate: a landlord often prefers keeping a reliable tenant over a vacancy, so ask them to hold or soften the increase.

Before signing, ask exactly what's due at move-in (some places skip last-month or reduce the deposit), and have that full amount saved.
